fields.title: 1 Kings
fields.subtitle: Melakhim Alef, “Kings”
fields.description: The first half of the book of Kings, which opens with King David too old to keep warm and closes with Ahab’s son bowing to Baal. Solomon asks for a heart that listens and is given wisdom beyond all the kings of the earth; he builds the temple, the cloud of glory fills it, and he prays, “will God really live on earth?” Then his heart turns, the kingdom tears in two, and Jeroboam sets up golden calves. And into the darkness of Ahab and Jezebel walks Elijah: ravens by the brook, the widow’s jar of flour, fire on Mount Carmel, and a faint sound, thin as silence, on the mountain of God. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of 1 Kings?
qa.answer: The first half of the book of Kings in the Old Testament, which tells the history of Israel’s kings from the death of David, around 970 BC, to the middle of the ninth century BC. In Hebrew Kings is one book, called Melakhim, “Kings”; the ancient Greek translation divided it in two. Its twenty-two chapters fall into three parts: the reign of Solomon and the building of the temple (1–11), the division of the kingdom into Israel in the north and Judah in the south (12–16), and the ministry of the prophet Elijah in the days of King Ahab (17–22).

qa.question: Who wrote 1 and 2 Kings, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Kings to the prophet Jeremiah. Many scholars see it as the closing part of a history running from Deuteronomy through Kings, shaped by Deuteronomy’s teaching and given its final form during the exile in Babylon, since 2 Kings ends with an event of about 561 BC. The writer names older sources he drew on, such as “the Book of the Acts of Solomon” and the histories of the kings of Israel and of Judah, which are now lost.

qa.question: Why did Israel split into two kingdoms?
qa.answer: 1 Kings gives two reasons, one human and one divine. When Solomon’s son Rehoboam refused to lighten the heavy labour his father had laid on the people, the northern tribes rejected him and made Jeroboam their king (chapter 12). But the book traces the break back to Solomon’s own heart: in old age his foreign wives turned him to other gods, and the LORD told him the kingdom would be torn from his son, leaving one tribe for the sake of David and Jerusalem (11:4–13). From then on there were two kingdoms: Israel in the north and Judah, ruled by David’s line, in the south.

qa.question: Who was Elijah?
qa.answer: A prophet, “Elijah the Tishbite”, from Gilead east of the Jordan, who opposed King Ahab and Queen Jezebel when they made the worship of Baal the religion of the court in the ninth century BC. His name means “My God is the LORD”. In 1 Kings he announces a drought, is fed by ravens and by a widow at Zarephath, raises her son, calls down fire on Mount Carmel, flees to Horeb, and confronts Ahab over the murder of Naboth. In 2 Kings he is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind. The New Testament sees his spirit in John the Baptist, shows him with Jesus at the transfiguration, and holds him up as an example of prayer (James 5:17–18).

qa.question: What is the “still small voice” in 1 Kings 19?
qa.answer: The words older English Bibles use for the way God came to Elijah at Horeb, after a wind, an earthquake and a fire in which the LORD was not present (19:11–12). The Hebrew means something like “a sound of thin silence”, and this translation renders it “a faint sound, thin as silence”. The scene comes just after Elijah’s triumph on Carmel, when he has fled for his life and asked to die. God answers his despair with food, rest, quiet, a new task and the news that seven thousand in Israel have stayed faithful.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. “LORD” in capitals stands for God’s personal name. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
But will God really live on earth? Heaven itself, even the highest heaven, cannot contain you. How much less this house that I have built!

— 1 Kings 8:27

1 Kings opens with an old man who cannot get warm. King David, the shepherd who faced a giant and sang the psalms, lies in bed under heaps of clothes while his sons manoeuvre for his throne. It closes, twenty-two chapters later, with a king of Israel bleeding to death in his chariot, dogs licking up his blood, and a son on the throne who “served Baal and worshiped him”. Between those two scenes lies a golden age and its undoing.

In Hebrew the book is called Melakhim, “Kings”, and it is the first half of a single work. The ancient Greek translation counted Samuel and Kings together as four books of “Kingdoms” and cut Kings in two, which is why 2 Kings begins in the middle of a reign. The story it tells runs from about 970 BC, when Solomon came to the throne, to about 850 BC, in the days of Ahab’s sons.

It is a book about kings, but its real subject is a King. Every ruler in it is measured by one question: did he do what was right in the sight of the LORD? And its most powerful figures are not the men on thrones but the prophets who walk in and say, “The LORD says this.”

Three movements

1 Kings falls into three parts. Chapters 1–11 belong to Solomon: his rise, his wisdom, the temple he built and the heart that turned away. Chapters 12–16 tell how the kingdom tore in two and follow both halves, king by king, through half a century of short reigns and violent ends. Chapters 17–22 slow down to follow one prophet, Elijah, in his long contest with King Ahab and Queen Jezebel.

The pace changes sharply. Solomon’s forty years fill eleven chapters; then kings rise and fall in a sentence or two, and Zimri reigns for seven days. Then the book all but stops to watch a man on a mountain, praying for fire.

A heart that listens

Solomon does not come to the throne gently. His older brother Adonijah declares, “I will be king,” Nathan and Bathsheba hurry to remind David of his promise, and Solomon is anointed while the people shout, “Long live King Solomon!” Once David is dead, the new king removes his rivals one by one, and the narrator notes without comment, “So the kingdom was made secure in Solomon’s hand.”

Then, at Gibeon, the LORD appears to the young king in a dream and makes an astonishing offer: “Ask for whatever you want me to give you.” Solomon calls himself “only a little boy” who does not know “how to go out and come in as a leader”, and asks:

So give your servant a heart that listens, to judge your people and to tell good from evil. For who is able to judge so great a people as yours?”

— 1 Kings 3:9

“It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked for this.” He is given wisdom, and riches and honour besides. The next story shows the wisdom at work: two women, one living baby, and a king who calls for a sword and lets a mother’s love reveal the truth. His understanding is “as vast as the sand on the seashore” (4:29). And the old promise to Abraham seems to have come true at last: “Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea; they ate and drank and were glad.”

A house for the name

The centre of Solomon’s reign is the temple. It was begun, the book says, in the 480th year after Israel came out of Egypt, and it was built in reverent quiet: the stones were dressed at the quarry, “so the sound of hammer, axe or any iron tool was never heard at the temple during the building.” When the ark is carried into the inner room, the cloud of God’s presence fills the house so thickly that the priests cannot stand to do their work, “since the house of the LORD was full of the glory of the LORD.”

Then Solomon spreads out his hands toward heaven and prays one of the great prayers of the Old Testament (8:22–53). Its heart is the verse that heads this introduction. The king who has just built the finest house in Israel knows that it cannot hold its Owner. What the temple can be is a place toward which people pray, and so the prayer becomes a long plea that God will listen: “Hear in heaven, your dwelling place; and when you hear, forgive.”

Solomon imagines every kind of trouble: drought, famine, defeat, the foreigner who comes from far away because of God’s name, and finally the worst of all, the people carried off into exile, since “there is no one who never sins.” Even then, he asks, if they turn back and pray toward this land, hear and forgive. For the exiles who first read the finished book, this prayer was a lifeline. Its goal is wider than Israel: “so that every people on earth may know that the LORD is God and that there is no other.”

When the queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with hard questions, she leaves overwhelmed: “I was not told even half.” For a moment Israel is what it was meant to be, a light that draws the nations.

The heart that turned

But the shadows are there for anyone who reads closely. Deuteronomy had warned that a king must not build up horses from Egypt, or take many wives, “or his heart will be led astray”, or pile up silver and gold. Chapter 10 lists Solomon’s gold and his horses from Egypt; chapter 11 counts his wives. The sentence that follows is one of the saddest in the Old Testament:

When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart to follow other gods, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of his father David had been.

— 1 Kings 11:4

The wisest man in the world was not kept safe by his wisdom. The LORD tells him, “I will certainly tear the kingdom from you and give it to your servant.” Yet even in judgement there is mercy: one tribe will be left to his son “because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” The prophet Ahijah tears a new cloak into twelve pieces and hands ten to Jeroboam, one of Solomon’s officials. The one left is kept for David’s sake, “so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem”. That small lamp will burn through the rest of Kings.

The kingdom torn in two

When Solomon dies, his son Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, and the northern tribes ask him to lighten the heavy labour his father laid on them. The old advisers tell him to be a servant to the people; his young friends tell him to show them who is master. He follows the young men: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will make your yoke heavier still.” The north answers with an old cry of rebellion: “What part do we have in David?”

From here on there are two kingdoms. Israel, in the north, has ten tribes and, later, its capital at Samaria; Judah, in the south, has Jerusalem, the temple and David’s line. Jeroboam, the north’s first king, fears that if his people keep going up to Jerusalem to worship, their hearts will go with them. So he gives them shrines of their own:

So the king took counsel and made two golden calves. He said to the people, “You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Israel, here are your gods, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!”

— 1 Kings 12:28

The words are almost exactly those spoken over Aaron’s golden calf at the foot of Sinai (Exodus 32:4), and the book means us to hear the echo. “This thing became a sin.” It is worship arranged for the safety of the state, and it becomes the north’s original sin. King after king of Israel is condemned for walking “in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin, by which he had led Israel to sin.”

Weighed against David

From chapter 14 on, the book settles into a pattern. Each king is introduced by the year of his neighbour’s reign in which he came to the throne, his age and the length of his reign are given, and then comes the verdict. Kings of Israel are measured against Jeroboam; kings of Judah against David. Asa “did what was right in the sight of the LORD, as his ancestor David had done”, though, the book adds, “The high places, however, were not taken away.” Of others the book says only that they did evil.

This is not the history a court chronicler would have written. Omri, who founded Samaria and was so powerful that Assyrian inscriptions went on calling Israel “the house of Omri” long after his line had ended, gets six verses. For his battles the reader is sent elsewhere, to “the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel”. What Kings wants to know is not how strong a king was but whether he was faithful.

And it watches for the word of the LORD coming true. A man of God from Judah cries out against Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel that a son of David named Josiah will one day burn human bones on it (13:2), and three hundred years later, in 2 Kings, he does. When Jericho is rebuilt at the cost of the builder’s sons, the narrator adds, “as the word of the LORD had said through Joshua son of Nun.” Kings make their plans, but the prophets’ word is what stands.

Elijah

Then Ahab comes to the throne, who “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him”. He marries Jezebel, a princess of Sidon, and builds a temple of Baal in Samaria. Baal was worshipped as the storm god, the giver of rain and harvest. And into that world, with no introduction and no ancestry, walks a man whose name means “My God is the LORD”:

Elijah the Tishbite, one of the settlers in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, whom I serve, there will be neither dew nor rain in the years ahead unless I give the word.”

— 1 Kings 17:1

The drought is aimed at Baal on his own ground. For three years there is no rain, and God feeds his prophet by unlikely means: ravens bring him bread and meat by a stream, and then he is sent to a widow in Zarephath, in Sidon, Jezebel’s own country. She has “only a handful of flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug”, and is gathering sticks to cook a last meal for her son and herself. She shares it, and “the jar of flour was not emptied, and the jug of oil did not give out”. When her son dies, Elijah stretches himself over the boy and cries to the LORD, and the child lives. Jesus would later remind his home town that of all the widows in Israel, Elijah was sent to this foreigner (Luke 4:25–26).

Fire on Carmel

In the third year Elijah confronts Ahab and calls the people and the prophets of Baal to Mount Carmel. There he puts the question that the whole book has been asking:

Elijah stepped up before all the people and said, “How long will you go on hobbling between two choices? If the LORD is God, follow him. If it is Baal, follow Baal.” But the people said nothing in reply.

— 1 Kings 18:21

The prophets of Baal call on their god from morning until noon, “But no sound came, and no one answered.” Elijah mocks them: perhaps their god “has fallen asleep, and must be woken up!” Then, at the time of the evening offering, he rebuilds the LORD’s broken altar with twelve stones, drenches it with water, and prays a short, plain prayer: “Answer me, the LORD, answer me, so that these people may know that you, the LORD, are God and are turning their hearts back again.” The fire falls and consumes even the stones.

When all the people saw it, they fell face down and said, “The LORD, he is God! The LORD, he is God!”

— 1 Kings 18:39

The day ends in blood, with the prophets of Baal put to death at the Kishon River. It is a hard scene. It carries out the sentence the law of Moses laid on prophets who led Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:5), and Christians have not taken it as a pattern for the church: when James and John later wanted to call down fire from heaven, Jesus “gave them a stern rebuke” (Luke 9:54–55). Then Elijah climbs the mountain again, bows to the ground and prays for rain, sending his servant to look out to sea seven times until “a cloud as small as a man’s hand” rises out of it. The letter of James takes the lesson: “Elijah was a human being just like us.”

A faint sound, thin as silence

The next chapter is one of the most human in the Bible. After the greatest victory of his life, a single threat from Jezebel sends Elijah running for his life into the wilderness. He sits under a broom tree and asks to die. “It is enough,” he says. “Now, LORD, take my life, for I am no better than my ancestors.” God’s first answer is not a rebuke but sleep and food, twice: “Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you.”

He walks forty days to Horeb, the mountain where God gave the law to Moses, and there God asks him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?” Elijah pours out his complaint: he alone is left. Then the LORD passes by. A great wind splits the mountains, but the LORD is not in the wind, nor in the earthquake that follows.

Then came fire after the earthquake, but the LORD was not in the fire. And when the fire had passed, a faint sound, thin as silence.

— 1 Kings 19:12

The God who answered by fire on Carmel now comes in something almost too quiet to hear. He does not argue with his tired servant. He gives him work to do, among it the anointing of Elisha to take his place, and corrects him gently: he is not alone. “Yet I will leave 7,000 in Israel, everyone whose knees have not bent to Baal.” Paul would recall those seven thousand when he wrote that there is always a remnant, “chosen by grace” (Romans 11:4–5).

A vineyard and a vision

The last chapters show what kind of king Ahab is. He wants Naboth’s vineyard; Naboth refuses to sell his family’s inheritance. Jezebel has him falsely accused and stoned, and when Ahab goes down to take the vineyard, Elijah is waiting. “Have you found me, my enemy?” says the king. “I have found you,” comes the answer. And yet, when Ahab tears his clothes and humbles himself, God delays the judgement. There is mercy even for Ahab.

The book ends with a prophet who will not say what the king wants to hear. Four hundred court prophets promise Ahab victory at Ramoth-gilead; Micaiah son of Imlah, whom Ahab hates “for his prophecies about me are never good”, says, “whatever the LORD says to me is what I will speak.” His vision of a lying spirit sent among Ahab’s prophets has puzzled readers; many take it to mean that God gave Ahab over to the falsehood he preferred, and notice that Micaiah tells him so to his face, a last warning. Ahab goes into battle in disguise, and “a man drew his bow at random”. No disguise can hide a king from the word of the LORD.

How to read 1 Kings

Read it with 2 Kings, which picks up the story mid-sentence. Do not worry about remembering every king of the north: notice the verdict on each, and watch for the prophets, who appear at every turning point. The books of Chronicles tell much of the same story, from Judah’s side and with different emphases; reading the two together is like hearing two witnesses.

The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, credited Kings to the prophet Jeremiah. Many scholars see it as the last part of a long history running from Deuteronomy through Kings and shaped by Deuteronomy’s teaching, given its final form during the exile, since 2 Kings ends in about 561 BC. The writer names his sources, royal annals now lost, and Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions name Omri, Ahab and Jehu. The reign lengths and cross-dates are famously hard to fit together; overlapping reigns and different ways of counting a king’s first year explain much of the difficulty, and Christians hold a range of views on the details.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Kings are worth knowing.

“The LORD” and “the Lord.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation follows long custom and writes “the LORD”. Where it uses the title Adonai, “Lord”, as it does when “It pleased the Lord” that Solomon asked for wisdom, it writes “Lord”. The old title “LORD of hosts” appears as “the LORD of Armies” (and “LORD God of hosts” as “the LORD God of Armies”).

Hobbling. At Carmel the same Hebrew verb describes the people “hobbling between two choices” and the prophets of Baal “hobbling in a dance around the altar”. The translation keeps the echo: a people that will not choose ends up limping like the priests of a god who does not answer.

The voice at Horeb. The famous “still small voice” of older translations is, in Hebrew, something like “a sound of thin silence”. This translation renders it “a faint sound, thin as silence”.

“Rested with his ancestors.” The phrase older translations gave as “slept with his fathers” closes each reign; here it reads “rested with his ancestors”.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Kings 1
fields.body_html:
Adonijah claims the throne

King David was now old, well on in years. They covered him with clothes, but he could not keep warm. So his officials said to him, “Let a young virgin be found for my lord the king, to wait on the king and look after him. Let her lie in your arms, so that my lord the king may keep warm.” So they searched throughout the land of Israel for a beautiful young woman. They found Abishag the Shunammite, and they brought her to the king. The young woman was very beautiful. She looked after the king and waited on him, but the king had no sexual relations with her. Now Adonijah son of Haggith was putting himself forward, saying, “I will be king.” He got himself chariots and horsemen, with fifty men to run ahead of him. His father had never once crossed him by asking, “Why have you done this?” He was also very handsome, and he was born next after Absalom. He conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, and they gave Adonijah their support. But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei and David’s own warriors did not side with Adonijah. Adonijah sacrificed sheep, cattle and fattened calves at the Stone of Zoheleth, near En-rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah who were the king’s officials. But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the warriors, or his brother Solomon. Then Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother, “Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, without our lord David knowing anything about it? Now come, let me give you some advice, so that you can save your own life and the life of your son Solomon. Go in to King David and say to him, ‘My lord the king, did you not swear to your servant, “Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne”? So why has Adonijah become king?’ Then, while you are still there talking to the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words.” So Bathsheba went in to the king in his room. He was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending him. Bathsheba bowed low before the king, and the king asked, “What do you want?” She said to him, “My lord, you yourself swore to your servant by the LORD your God, ‘Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne.’ But now Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, do not even know it. He has sacrificed great numbers of cattle, fattened calves and sheep, and has invited all the king’s sons, Abiathar the priest and Joab the commander of the army. But he has not invited your servant Solomon. And you, my lord the king: all Israel has its eyes on you, waiting for you to tell them who will sit on my lord the king’s throne after him. Otherwise, when my lord the king rests with his ancestors, my son Solomon and I will be treated as criminals.” While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet arrived. The king was told, “Nathan the prophet is here.” So he came in before the king and bowed down to him with his face to the ground. Nathan said, “My lord the king, did you say, ‘Adonijah will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne’? For today he has gone down and sacrificed great numbers of cattle, fattened calves and sheep. He has invited all the king’s sons, the commanders of the army and Abiathar the priest. Right now they are eating and drinking in his presence and shouting, ‘Long live King Adonijah!’ But he did not invite me, your servant, or Zadok the priest, or Benaiah son of Jehoiada, or your servant Solomon. Has my lord the king done this without letting your servant know who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?”

David promises the throne to Solomon

Then King David answered, “Call Bathsheba back to me.” So she came into the king’s presence and stood before him. Then the king swore an oath: “As surely as the LORD lives, who has rescued my life from every trouble, I will do today exactly what I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel: ‘Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place.’” Bathsheba bowed down with her face to the ground, paying honor to the king, and said, “May my lord King David live forever!”

Solomon is anointed king

Then King David said, “Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me.” So they came before the king. The king said to them, “Take your lord’s officials with you. Have my son Solomon ride on my own mule, and take him down to Gihon. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet are to anoint him there as king over Israel. Then blow the ram’s horn and shout, ‘Long live King Solomon!’ Then come back up after him, and he is to come and sit on my throne. He will be king in my place, for I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and Judah.” Benaiah son of Jehoiada answered the king, “Amen! May the LORD, the God of my lord the king, say so too. As the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may he be with Solomon, and may he make his throne even greater than the throne of my lord King David!” So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites went down. They had Solomon ride on King David’s mule and brought him to Gihon. Zadok the priest brought the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon with it. Then they blew the ram’s horn, and all the people shouted, “Long live King Solomon!” Then all the people went up after him, playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy, so that the ground shook with their noise. Adonijah and all the guests with him heard it just as they finished eating. When Joab heard the sound of the ram’s horn, he said, “Why is the city in such an uproar?” While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, “Come in. You are a worthy man, and you must be bringing good news.” Jonathan answered Adonijah, “Not at all! Our lord King David has made Solomon king. The king sent with him Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and the Pelethites, and they had him ride on the king’s mule. Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him king at Gihon. From there they have come up rejoicing, and the city is in an uproar. That is the noise you heard. What is more, Solomon has taken his seat on the royal throne. Besides that, the king’s officials have come to congratulate our lord King David, saying, ‘May God make Solomon’s name more famous than yours, and his throne greater than yours!’ And the king bowed in worship on his bed. And the king also said this: ‘Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has today given me one to sit on my throne, and has let me see it with my own eyes.’” Then all Adonijah’s guests got up in alarm, and each of them went his own way. Adonijah was afraid of Solomon, so he got up, went and took hold of the horns of the altar. Solomon was told, “Adonijah is afraid of King Solomon. He has taken hold of the horns of the altar and is saying, ‘Let King Solomon first swear to me today that he will not put his servant to death with the sword.’” Solomon said, “If he proves to be a worthy man, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if any wrong is found in him, he will die.” Then King Solomon sent men to bring him down from the altar. Adonijah came and bowed before King Solomon, and Solomon told him, “Go home.”
fields.summary: As David grows old, his son Adonijah declares himself king. Nathan and Bathsheba remind David of his promise, and David has Solomon anointed king at Gihon.

fields.title: 1 Kings 2
fields.body_html:
David’s last charge to Solomon

When the time came near for David to die, he gave a charge to his son Solomon: “I am going the way of all the earth. Be strong, then, and show yourself a man. Keep what the LORD your God has entrusted to you: walk in his ways and keep his statutes, his commandments, his rulings, and his decrees, as they are written in the law of Moses. Then you will act wisely and succeed in all you do and wherever you turn, so that the LORD may keep the promise he made about me: ‘If your descendants watch how they live, walking faithfully before me with all their heart and all their soul, there will always be a man of your line on the throne of Israel.’ You also know how Joab son of Zeruiah treated me, and what he did to the two commanders of Israel’s armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them, spilling blood in a time of peace as though it were war, and he stained the belt at his waist and the sandals on his feet with that blood of war. Act as your wisdom tells you, but do not allow his gray head to go down in peace to Sheol.

But show faithful love to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite; give them a place among those who eat at your table, for they came to my side in just that way when I was fleeing from your brother Absalom. There is also Shimei son of Gera with you, the Benjaminite from Bahurim. He hurled bitter curses at me on the day I set out for Mahanaim. But he came down to the Jordan to meet me, and I gave him my oath by the LORD: ‘I will not put you to death with the sword.’ But now, do not treat him as innocent. You are a wise man; you will know what to do to him. Bring his gray head down to Sheol in blood.” Then David rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David.

The death of David

David’s reign over Israel lasted forty years: seven of them he reigned in Hebron, and thirty-three in Jerusalem. So Solomon took his seat on the throne of his father David, and his royal rule was made very firm. Then Adonijah son of Haggith came to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother. She asked, “Have you come in peace?” “Yes, in peace,” he answered. Then he said, “I have something to say to you.” “Say it,” she replied. He said, “You know that the kingship was mine. All Israel looked to me to be king. But the kingship changed hands and went to my brother, because it came to him from the LORD. Now I have one request to ask of you. Do not refuse me.” “Say it,” she replied. He said, “Please ask King Solomon, for he will not refuse you, to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.” “Very well,” said Bathsheba. “I will speak on your behalf to the king.” So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him on behalf of Adonijah. The king stood up to meet her and bowed down to her. Then he sat down on his throne and had a throne set for the king’s mother, and she sat at his right hand. She said, “I have one small request to ask of you. Do not refuse me.” The king answered her, “Ask, my mother, for I will not refuse you.” She said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given in marriage to your brother Adonijah.” King Solomon answered his mother, “Why are you asking for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? You might as well ask for the kingdom for him, since he is my older brother. Ask it for him, and for Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah too!”

Solomon deals with Adonijah, Abiathar and Joab

Then King Solomon swore by the LORD, “May God deal with me ever so severely if this request does not cost Adonijah his life! Now, as surely as the LORD lives, who has made me secure and seated me on the throne of my father David, and has made me a house as he promised, Adonijah will be put to death today!” So King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck Adonijah down, and he died.

To Abiathar the priest the king said, “Go to your fields at Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I will not put you to death now, because you bore the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David and shared in all the hardships my father endured.” So Solomon removed Abiathar from serving as priest of the LORD. This fulfilled the word the LORD had spoken about the house of Eli at Shiloh.

When the news reached Joab, since he had sided with Adonijah, though he had not sided with Absalom, Joab fled to the tent of the LORD and grasped the horns of the altar. King Solomon was told that Joab had fled to the tent of the LORD and was there beside the altar. Then Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada with the order, “Go and strike him down.” Benaiah went to the tent of the LORD and said to him, “The king says this: ‘Come out!’” But he said, “No, I will die here.” Benaiah took word back to the king: “This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me.” The king said to him, “Do as he said. Strike him down and bury him, and so take away from me and from my father’s house the guilt of the blood that Joab shed without cause. The LORD will bring his blood back on his own head, because without my father David’s knowledge he attacked two men more righteous and better than himself and killed them with the sword: Abner son of Ner, commander of the army of Israel, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of the army of Judah. So their blood will come back on Joab’s head and on the heads of his descendants forever. But for David and his descendants, his house and his throne, there will be peace from the LORD forever.” So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up and struck him down and killed him, and he was buried at his own home in the wilderness. The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada over the army in Joab’s place, and he put Zadok the priest in Abiathar’s place. Then the king summoned Shimei and told him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and make your home there. Do not leave it to go anywhere at all. On the day you go out and cross the Kidron Valley, you may be certain you will die. Your blood will be on your own head.” Shimei answered the king, “What you say is fair. Your servant will do just as my lord the king has said.” So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for a long time.

The death of Shimei

But three years later two slaves belonging to Shimei ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei was told, “Your slaves are in Gath.” So Shimei got up, saddled his donkey, and went to Achish at Gath to look for his slaves. Shimei went and brought his slaves back from Gath. Word reached Solomon that Shimei had left Jerusalem for Gath and had come back. Then the king summoned Shimei and said to him, “Did I not have you swear by the LORD, and did I not warn you, ‘The day you leave and go anywhere at all, you can be sure that you will die’? And you said to me, ‘What you say is fair; I will obey.’ Why then have you failed to keep your oath to the LORD and the command I gave you?” The king also said to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the wrong you did to my father David. Now the LORD will bring your wrongdoing back on your own head. But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will stand firm before the LORD forever.” Then the king gave the order to Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who went out and struck Shimei down, and he died. So the kingdom was made secure in Solomon’s hand.
fields.summary: David charges Solomon to keep God’s ways and dies. Solomon secures his throne: Adonijah, Joab and Shimei are put to death, and Abiathar is sent away.

fields.title: 1 Kings 3
fields.body_html:
Solomon asks for wisdom

Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He married Pharaoh’s daughter and brought her to live in the city of David until he had finished building his own palace, the house of the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem. The people, however, were still offering sacrifices at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD in those days.

Solomon loved the LORD and lived by the statutes of his father David, except that he too offered sacrifices and burned offerings at the high places. The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, because it was the most important high place. On that altar Solomon offered up a thousand burnt offerings. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream at night. God said, “Ask for whatever you want me to give you.” Solomon answered, “You showed great faithful love to your servant, my father David, because he lived his life before you with faithfulness and righteousness and an upright heart. And you have kept this great faithful love for him by giving him a son to sit on his throne, as he does today. Now, the LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of my father David. But I am only a little boy; I do not know how to go out and come in as a leader. And your servant is here among your chosen people, a people so great that they cannot be numbered or counted. So give your servant a heart that listens, to judge your people and to tell good from evil. For who is able to judge so great a people as yours?” It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked for this. So God said to him, “Because you have asked for this, and have not asked for a long life for yourself, or wealth, or the death of your enemies, but have asked for understanding so that you can listen to cases and judge them justly, So I will do what you have asked. I am giving you a wise and discerning heart. No one before you has been like you, and no one after you will ever rise up who is like you. I am also giving you what you did not ask for: both wealth and honor. As long as you live, no other king will be your equal. And if you walk in my ways and keep my statutes and my commandments, as your father David did, I will give you a long life.”

Then Solomon woke up and realized it had been a dream. He went to Jerusalem, and there he stood before the ark of the Lord’s covenant. He offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and held a feast for all his officials.

Solomon judges between two mothers

Some time later two prostitutes came to the king and stood in his presence. The first woman said, “Please, my lord, this woman and I share one house. I had a baby while she was there with me. Three days after my child was born, this woman also had a baby. We were alone; there was no one else with us in the house, just the two of us. This woman’s son died in the night, because she lay on top of him. So in the middle of the night she rose and took my son from my side while your servant slept. She laid him in her arms, and she laid her dead son in my arms. When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, he was dead! But when I looked at him closely in the morning light, I saw that he was not the son I had given birth to.” But the other woman said, “No! The living one is my son, and the dead one is yours.” The first woman kept saying, “No! The dead one is your son, and the living one is mine.” And so they argued before the king. The king said, “This one says, ‘My son is the one who is alive, and your son is dead,’ and that one says, ‘No! Your son is dead, and mine is alive.’”

Then the king said, “Bring me a sword.” So they brought a sword to the king. Then the king said, “Cut the living child in two, and give half to one woman and half to the other.” Then the mother of the living child spoke to the king, for her love for her son burned within her. “Please, my lord,” she said, “let her have the living baby! Do not put him to death!” But the other woman kept saying, “He shall belong to neither of us. Cut him in two!” Then the king answered, “Let the woman who pleaded for him have the living baby. Do not put him to death. She is his mother.” All Israel heard about the judgment the king had given, and they held him in awe, for they saw that God’s wisdom was in him, so that he could do justice.
fields.summary: At Gibeon God appears to Solomon in a dream, and Solomon asks for an understanding heart to govern the people. God gives him wisdom, riches and honor, and Solomon judges between two women who claim the same baby.

fields.title: 1 Kings 4
fields.body_html:
Solomon’s officials

King Solomon ruled as king over all Israel.

These were his high officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest;

Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, served as secretaries; the recorder was Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud; Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests;

Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the district governors; Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king’s friend; Ahishar was in charge of the palace, and Adoniram son of Abda had charge of the forced labor.

Solomon’s twelve district governors

Solomon had twelve district governors over all Israel, who supplied food for the king and his household. Each of them had to provide for one month in the year.

These are their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;

Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan;

Ben-hesed, in Arubboth; Socoh and all the land of Hepher were his;

Ben-abinadab, all Naphath-dor (Taphath, Solomon’s daughter, was his wife);

Baana son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo and all Beth-shean beside Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and on beyond Jokmeam;

Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead. The villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead were his, and so was the region of Argob in Bashan: sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars;

Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he too had married a daughter of Solomon, Basemath); Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;

Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar;

Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin;

Geber son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the territory of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. In the land there was one governor. Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea; they ate and drank and were glad. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and as far as the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon throughout his life.

Solomon’s provisions for a single day were about 180 bushels of fine flour and about 360 bushels of meal, ten fattened cattle, twenty cattle from the pasture and a hundred sheep and goats, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened birds. For he had dominion over the whole region west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates, and he had peace on every side all around him. Judah and Israel lived in safety, everyone under their own vine and under their own fig tree, from Dan to Beersheba, all through Solomon’s lifetime.

Solomon had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. These officers provided for King Solomon and for everyone who came to King Solomon’s table, each in his month. They saw to it that nothing was lacking. They also brought barley and straw for the horses and the swift horses to the place where it was needed, each according to his assignment.

God gave Solomon wisdom and very great understanding, and a breadth of mind as vast as the sand on the seashore. Solomon’s wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the peoples of the east and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt. He was wiser than anyone else, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His fame spread to all the surrounding nations. He spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs numbered 1,005. He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing out of the wall, and he spoke about animals, birds, creeping things and fish.

Solomon’s rule and wisdom

People came from all the nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom; they came on behalf of all the kings of the earth, who had heard how wise he was.
fields.summary: Solomon’s officials and the district governors who supply the royal household are listed.

fields.title: 1 Kings 5
fields.body_html:
Hiram supplies wood for the temple

Hiram king of Tyre sent his officials to Solomon when he heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father’s place, for Hiram had always been a friend of David.

Solomon sent word to Hiram: “You know that my father David could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the wars waged against him on every side, until the LORD put his enemies under the soles of his feet. But now the LORD my God has given me rest all around. I have no adversary and face no misfortune. So I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, just as the LORD told my father David: ‘Your son, whom I will put on your throne in your place, will build the house for my name.’ So now give orders for cedars from Lebanon to be cut for me. My servants will work with your servants, and I will pay you whatever wages you set for your servants. You know that none of us knows how to cut timber as well as the Sidonians do.” When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he was delighted and said, “Blessed be the LORD today, who has given David a wise son to rule over this great people!” Then Hiram sent word to Solomon: “I have received the message you sent me. I will do all you wish in the matter of cedar timber and cypress timber. My servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea, and I will have them tied into rafts and sent by sea to the place you name. There I will have them taken apart, and you can carry them away. And you will meet my wishes by providing food for my household.” So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the cedar timber and cypress timber he wished for. Solomon gave Hiram about 120,000 bushels of wheat as food for his household, and about 1,200 gallons of pressed olive oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year after year.

The LORD gave wisdom to Solomon, as he had promised him. Hiram and Solomon were at peace, and the two of them made a treaty with each other. King Solomon drafted forced labor from all Israel, and the labor force numbered 30,000 men. He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of 10,000 a month. They spent a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.

Solomon’s workers

Solomon also had 70,000 men who carried loads and 80,000 who cut stone in the hill country, besides Solomon’s 3,300 chief officers who were over the work and directed the people who did it. At the king’s command they quarried great, costly stones, so that the foundation of the house could be laid with dressed stone. Solomon’s builders and Hiram’s builders and the men of Gebal shaped the stones, and they prepared the timber and the stone for building the house.
fields.summary: Judah and Israel live in safety and plenty, and Solomon’s wisdom surpasses all others. Solomon makes an agreement with Hiram king of Tyre for cedar and cypress, and raises a labor force to build the house of God.

fields.title: 1 Kings 6
fields.body_html:
Solomon builds the temple

In the 480th year after the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year that Solomon reigned over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. The temple that King Solomon built for the LORD was about 90 feet long, about 30 feet wide and about 45 feet high. The porch in front of the main hall of the temple was about 30 feet long, matching the width of the temple, and it reached out about 15 feet from the front of the temple. He made windows for the temple with recessed frames. Against the wall of the temple he built a side structure that ran all around it, along the walls of both the main hall and the inner sanctuary, and he made side rooms all around. The lowest story was about 7 1/2 feet wide, the middle one about 9 feet wide, and the third about 10 1/2 feet wide. He had made ledges around the outside of the temple wall, so that the beams would not be set into the walls of the temple. The temple was built of stone that had been dressed at the quarry, so the sound of hammer, axe or any iron tool was never heard at the temple during the building. The entrance to the middle story of side rooms was on the south side of the temple, and stairways led up to the middle story and from the middle to the third. So he built the temple and finished it, and he roofed it with beams and planks of cedar. He built the side structure against the whole temple, each story about 7 1/2 feet high, and joined it to the temple with cedar beams.

The LORD speaks to Solomon

Then the word of the LORD came to Solomon: “As for this house you are building, if you live by my statutes, carry out my rulings and keep all my commandments by following them, I will carry out through you the word I gave to David your father, and I will live among the Israelites and will not abandon my people Israel.”

The inside of the temple

So Solomon built the temple and finished it. He lined the inside walls of the temple with cedar boards, paneling them with wood from the floor of the temple up to the rafters of the ceiling, and he covered the floor of the temple with boards of cypress. He partitioned off about 30 feet at the back of the temple with cedar boards from the floor to the rafters, and built it inside as the inner sanctuary, the most holy place. The rest of the temple, the main hall in front of the inner sanctuary, was about 60 feet long. Inside, the temple’s cedar was carved with gourds and open flowers. It was all cedar; no stone showed. He prepared the inner sanctuary inside the temple to place the ark of the covenant of the LORD there. The inner sanctuary was about 30 feet long, about 30 feet wide and about 30 feet high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar. Inside the temple Solomon overlaid everything with pure gold. He drew gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary, which he also overlaid with gold. So he overlaid the whole temple with gold until it was all finished. He also overlaid with gold the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary. He made two cherubim of olive wood for the inner sanctuary, each about 15 feet high. One wing of the cherub was about 7 1/2 feet long and the other wing about 7 1/2 feet, so its wings spanned about 15 feet from wingtip to wingtip. The second cherub also measured about 15 feet. The two cherubim were the same size and the same shape. The height of one cherub was about 15 feet, and so was the other. He placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner sanctuary of the temple. Their wings were spread out, so that the wing of one touched one wall and the wing of the other touched the other wall, while their wings met each other in the middle of the room. He also overlaid the cherubim with gold. On all the walls of the temple, all around, in both the inner and the outer rooms, he carved figures of cherubim, palm trees and open flowers. He also overlaid the floor of the temple with gold, in both the inner and the outer rooms. He made doors of olive wood for the entrance to the inner sanctuary, with a lintel and doorposts forming a five-sided frame. On the two olive-wood doors he carved cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold, beating the gold down onto the cherubim and the palm trees. In the same way he made doorposts of olive wood for the entrance of the main hall, in a four-sided frame. The two doors were of cypress wood. Each door had two leaves that folded. He carved cherubim, palm trees and open flowers on them, and overlaid them with gold fitted evenly over the carving. He built the inner courtyard with three courses of dressed stone and one course of cedar beams. In the fourth year, in the month of Ziv, the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid. In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the temple was finished in all its parts and just as it had been planned. He had been seven years building it.
fields.summary: Solomon builds the temple, its rooms and its inner sanctuary, lined with cedar and overlaid with gold. God promises to dwell among Israel if Solomon keeps God’s statutes, and the house is finished in seven years.

fields.title: 1 Kings 7
fields.body_html:
Solomon’s palace

Solomon was building his own palace for thirteen years, and then he finished the whole of it. He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon about 150 feet long, about 75 feet wide and about 45 feet high. It stood on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams laid on the pillars. It was roofed with cedar above the side rooms that rested on the pillars, forty-five rooms, fifteen in each row. There were window frames in three rows, and window faced window in three tiers. All the doorways and doorposts had square frames, and in front, window faced window in three tiers. He made the Hall of Pillars about 75 feet long and about 45 feet wide. There was a porch in front of it, and pillars with a canopy in front of that. He made the Hall of the Throne, where he was to judge, the Hall of Judgment. It was paneled with cedar from floor to ceiling. His own house where he was to live, in the other courtyard further in from the hall, was built the same way. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom he had married. All these buildings were made of costly stones, cut to size and sawn on their inner and outer faces, from the foundation up to the top course, and from the outside as far as the great courtyard. The foundations were laid with costly stones, large stones, some measuring about 15 feet and some about 12 feet. Above them were costly stones cut to size, and cedar beams. The great courtyard had walls all around of three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams, like the inner courtyard of the house of the LORD and the porch of the house.

Hiram makes the bronze pillars and the sea

King Solomon sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre. He was a widow’s son from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father had been a man of Tyre, a craftsman in bronze. Hiram was full of wisdom, understanding and knowledge for doing every kind of work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work. He cast the two bronze pillars. Each pillar was about 27 feet high, and it took a line of about 18 feet to go around it. He also made two capitals of cast bronze for the tops of the pillars. One capital was about 7 1/2 feet high, and the other capital was about 7 1/2 feet high. There were nets of lattice work and wreaths of chain work for the capitals on top of the pillars, seven for one capital and seven for the other. He made the pomegranates in two rows all around on the one network, to cover the capitals on top of the pillars, and he did the same for the other capital. The capitals on top of the pillars at the porch were lily work, about 6 feet high. The capitals on the two pillars were also above, close to the rounded part beside the network. There were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around, on the other capital as well. He erected the pillars at the temple porch. The pillar on the right he set up and named Jachin, and the pillar on the left he set up and named Boaz. On top of the pillars was lily work. So the work on the pillars was finished. He made the Sea of cast metal. It was round, about 15 feet from brim to brim and about 7 1/2 feet high, and it took a line of about 45 feet to measure around it. Under its brim, gourds went all around it, ten to every 18 inches, encircling the Sea. The gourds were in two rows, cast in one piece with it. It stood on twelve oxen: three faced north, three west, three south and three east. The Sea was set on top of them, and their hindquarters were all toward the center. It was about 3 inches thick, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like a lily blossom. It held about 12,000 gallons.

The bronze stands and basins

He also made ten bronze stands. Each stand was about 6 feet long, about 6 feet wide and about 4 1/2 feet high. This is how the stands were made: they had panels, and the panels were set between crossbars. On the panels between the crossbars were lions, oxen and cherubim. On the crossbars there was a base above, and below the lions and oxen were wreaths of hanging work. Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles, and its four feet had supports. The supports were cast to sit beneath the basin, and each had wreaths at its side. Its opening, within the crown, rose about 18 inches upward. The opening was round, made like a pedestal, about 27 inches across. There were carvings on its opening, and the panels were square, not round. The four wheels were under the panels, and the axles of the wheels were fixed to the stand. Each wheel was about 27 inches high. The wheels were made the way chariot wheels are made: axles, rims, spokes and hubs, all of cast metal. There were four supports at the four corners of each stand, and the supports were part of the stand itself. At the top of the stand was a round band about 9 inches high, and at the top of the stand its brackets and panels were one piece with it. On the surfaces of its brackets and on its panels he engraved cherubim, lions and palm trees, as each had space, with wreaths all around. This is how he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, with the same size and the same shape.

He made ten bronze basins. Each basin held about 240 gallons and measured about 6 feet across, with one basin on each of the ten stands. He placed five of the stands on the south side of the house and five on the north side. He put the Sea on the south side of the house, at the southeast corner.

The furnishings of the temple

Hiram also made the basins, the shovels and the sprinkling bowls. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD: the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars; the two networks covering the two bowls of the capitals on top of the pillars; the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, in two rows on each network, covering the two bowls of the capitals on top of the pillars; the ten stands, with the ten basins on the stands; the one Sea, with the twelve oxen under the Sea; and the pots, the shovels and the sprinkling bowls. All these things that Hiram made for King Solomon for the house of the LORD were of polished bronze. The king cast them in the clay ground of the Jordan plain, between Succoth and Zarethan. Solomon left all these things unweighed because there were so very many of them; the weight of the bronze was never found out. Solomon also made all the furnishings of the house of the LORD: the altar of gold; the table of gold for the bread of the Presence; the lampstands of pure gold, five on the right and five on the left in front of the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps and the tongs of gold; the cups, the wick trimmers, the sprinkling bowls, the dishes and the firepans of pure gold; and the gold sockets for the inner house doors, those of the most holy place, and for the doors to the main hall of the temple.

So all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. Then Solomon brought in the things his father David had dedicated, the silver, the gold and the vessels, and he put them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
fields.summary: Solomon builds his own palace over thirteen years. Hiram of Tyre makes the bronze pillars, the sea of cast metal and the furnishings of the temple.

fields.title: 1 Kings 8
fields.body_html:
The ark is brought into the temple

Then Solomon called together the elders of Israel, all the heads of the tribes and the leaders of the ancestral families of the Israelites, to come to King Solomon in Jerusalem. They were to bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD up from the city of David, that is, Zion. All the men of Israel gathered before King Solomon at the festival in the month of Ethanim, which is the seventh month. When all the elders of Israel had arrived, the priests picked up the ark. They brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy utensils that were in the tent. The priests and the Levites carried them up. King Solomon and the whole congregation of Israel who had gathered with him were in front of the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and cattle that they could not be counted or numbered. The priests then carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD into its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, the most holy place, under the wings of the cherubim. The cherubim spread their wings over the place where the ark stood, and so the cherubim formed a covering above the ark and its poles. The poles were so long that from the holy place, in front of the inner sanctuary, their ends were visible, though not from outside. They are still there to this day. The ark held nothing but the two stone tablets Moses had put in it at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the Israelites after they came out of the land of Egypt. As the priests were coming out of the holy place, the house of the LORD was filled by the cloud. The priests were unable to stand and do their service because of the cloud, since the house of the LORD was full of the glory of the LORD.

Solomon speaks to the people

Then Solomon said,
“The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.
I have indeed built a lofty house for you,
a place for you to dwell forever.”
Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel, while the whole assembly of Israel stood there. He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his own mouth made a promise to my father David and with his own hand has now fulfilled it. For he said, ‘Since the day I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I have chosen no city in any tribe of Israel in which to build a house where my name would be. But I chose David to rule over my people Israel.’ My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to my father David, ‘You wanted to build a house for my name, and you did well to have this in your heart. Yet you are not the one who will build the house. Your son, your own offspring, is the one who will build the house for my name.’ Now the LORD has kept the promise he made. I have taken the place of my father David and sit on Israel’s throne, as the LORD promised, and I have built this house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. There I have prepared a place for the ark, which holds the covenant of the LORD that he made with our ancestors when he brought them out of the land of Egypt.”

Solomon’s prayer of dedication

Then Solomon took his place before the altar of the LORD, in front of all the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven. He said, “The LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you in the heavens above or on the earth beneath. You keep your covenant and show faithful love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart, you who have kept for your servant, my father David, the promise you made to him. With your mouth you promised, and with your hand you have fulfilled it, as it is today. Now, the LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant, my father David, the promise you made to him: ‘You will never lack a man of your line sitting before me on the throne of Israel, as long as your descendants watch how they live and walk before me as you have walked before me.’ So now, God of Israel, please let the promise you made to your servant, my father David, be confirmed. But will God really live on earth? Heaven itself, even the highest heaven, cannot contain you. How much less this house that I have built! Yet listen to the prayer of your servant and to his plea for mercy, the LORD my God. Hear the cry and the prayer your servant prays before you this day, so that night and day your eyes may be open toward this house, toward the place about which you said, ‘My name will be there.’ Listen to the prayer that your servant prays toward this place. Listen to the pleading of your servant and your people Israel as they pray toward this place. Hear in heaven, your dwelling place; and when you hear, forgive. When someone sins against a neighbor and is required to take an oath, and comes and swears the oath before your altar in this house, then hear in heaven and act. Judge between your servants: condemn the guilty by bringing on his own head what he has done, and declare the innocent in the right by rewarding him for his righteousness.

When your people Israel are defeated by an enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn back to you, acknowledge your name, and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear in heaven and forgive your people Israel for their sin, and bring them back to the land you gave to their ancestors.

When the sky is shut and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, and they pray toward this place, acknowledge your name, and turn from their sin because you have humbled them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, as you teach them the good way to walk in. And send rain on your land, the land you gave to your people as their inheritance.

If there is famine in the land, or disease, or blight or mildew, locusts or grasshoppers, or if their enemy besieges them in any of their cities, whatever plague or sickness there is, whatever prayer or plea for mercy is made by anyone among all your people Israel, each one knowing the affliction of their own heart and spreading out their hands toward this house, then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive. Act, and give to each one according to all their ways, for you know each heart. You alone know every human heart, so that they will fear you all the days they live in the land you gave to our ancestors. As for the foreigner who is not one of your people Israel but comes from a distant land because of your name (for they will hear of your great name, your mighty hand, and your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house, then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, and do all that the foreigner asks of you. Then all the peoples of the earth will come to know your name and to fear you as your people Israel do, and to know that your name is called over this house I have built. When your people go out to fight against their enemy, wherever you send them, and they pray to the LORD facing the city you chose and the house I built for your name, then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause. When they sin against you (and there is no one who never sins), and you are angry with them and hand them over to an enemy, and their captors take them away as prisoners to the enemy’s land, whether far away or near, and they come to their senses in the land where they have been taken captive, and they turn back and plead with you in the land of those who took them captive, saying, ‘We have sinned; we have done wrong and acted wickedly,’ if they return to you with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies who carried them off, and pray to you facing their land, which you gave to their ancestors, the city you chose, and the house I built for your name, then hear in heaven, your dwelling place, their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all the rebellious acts they have committed against you. Grant them compassion in the sight of their captors, so that they will be merciful to them, for they are your people and your inheritance, whom you brought out of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, May your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, and may you hear them every time they cry out to you. For you set them apart from all the peoples of the earth to be your own inheritance, as you declared through your servant Moses when you brought our ancestors out of Egypt, Lord GOD.”

Solomon blesses the people

When Solomon had finished praying all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he got up from where he had been kneeling before the altar of the LORD, his hands spread out toward heaven. He stood up and called out a blessing on all the assembly of Israel, saying, “Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to his people Israel, just as he promised. Of all the good promises he made through his servant Moses, not one word has failed. May the LORD our God be with us just as he was with our ancestors. May he never leave us or abandon us, so that he may turn our hearts toward him, and we may walk in all his ways and keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rulings, which he commanded our ancestors. May these words I have prayed before the LORD stay near the LORD our God day and night, so that he upholds the cause of his servant and of his people Israel, day by day as each need arises, so that every people on earth may know that the LORD is God and that there is no other. So let your hearts be wholly true to the LORD our God, living by his statutes and keeping his commandments, as you are doing today.” Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD. Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 cattle and 120,000 sheep. In this way the king and all the Israelites dedicated the house of the LORD. That same day the king made holy the central part of the courtyard before the house of the LORD. He offered there the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat parts of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that stood before the LORD was too small to hold them: the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings. So at that time Solomon held the festival, and all Israel with him, a great assembly from Lebo-hamath to the Wadi of Egypt, before the LORD our God, for seven days and then seven more days, fourteen days in all. On the eighth day he sent the people away. They blessed the king and went home, joyful and glad at heart for all the good the LORD had done for David his servant and for Israel his people.
fields.summary: The ark is brought into the temple, and the cloud of God’s glory fills it. Solomon blesses the people and prays that God will hear prayers made toward this house, and the temple is dedicated with sacrifices and a festival.

fields.title: 1 Kings 9
fields.body_html:
The LORD appears to Solomon again

After Solomon had completed the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and everything else he had set his heart on making,

the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. The LORD said to him, “I have heard your prayer and the plea for mercy you made to me. I have set apart as holy this house you have built, and I have put my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will always be there. As for you, if you live before me as your father David did, with a whole heart and with uprightness, doing everything I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my rulings, then I will make the throne of your kingdom over Israel secure forever, as I promised your father David when I said, ‘There will always be a man of your line on the throne of Israel.’ But if you or your descendants turn away from following me, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, and instead go off to serve other gods and bow down to them, then I will cut Israel off from the land I have given them, and I will cast this house that I have made holy for my name out of my sight. Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all the peoples. And this house, high as it stands, will leave everyone who passes by it appalled. They will hiss and ask, ‘Why has the LORD dealt like this with this land and this house?’ And people will answer, ‘Because they abandoned the LORD their God, who brought their ancestors out of the land of Egypt, and they embraced other gods and worshiped and served them. That is why the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.’”

Solomon’s other works

At the end of the twenty years it took Solomon to build the two houses, the LORD’s house and the royal palace, since Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber and gold he wanted, King Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns in the region of Galilee. But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the towns Solomon had given him, they did not please him. He said, “What kind of towns are these you have given me, my brother?” So they have been called the land of Cabul to this day.

Hiram had sent the king about 9,000 pounds of gold. This is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon conscripted to build the house of the LORD, his own palace, the Millo, Jerusalem’s wall, and the cities of Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. Pharaoh king of Egypt had come up and captured Gezer. He burned it down, killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife. So Solomon rebuilt Gezer, and Lower Beth-horon, Baalath, and Tamar in the wilderness, within the land, and all the store cities that Solomon had, the towns for his chariots and for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout all the land he ruled. As for all the people who were left of the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, who were not Israelites, their descendants who were still left in the land, whom the Israelites had not been able to devote to destruction, Solomon conscripted as forced labor, as slaves, to this day. But Solomon did not make slaves of any of the Israelites. They were his soldiers, his officials, his commanders, his officers, and the commanders of his chariots and his horsemen.

These were the chief officers in charge of Solomon’s work: 550 of them, who directed the people doing the work. Once Pharaoh’s daughter had moved up from the city of David to the house Solomon had built for her, he built the Millo. Three times a year Solomon would present burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he himself had built for the LORD, and with them he burned incense before the LORD. And so he finished the house. King Solomon also built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, near Eloth in the land of Edom, on the shore of the Red Sea. Hiram sent his own servants with the fleet, sailors who knew the sea, to serve alongside Solomon’s servants. They went to Ophir and brought back from there about 31,500 pounds of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.
fields.summary: God appears to Solomon again, promising to keep his throne if he is faithful and warning of ruin if Israel turns away. Solomon’s building works, forced labor and fleet are described.

fields.title: 1 Kings 10
fields.body_html:
The queen of Sheba visits Solomon

The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame, a fame bound up with the name of the LORD, and she came to test him with difficult questions. She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large company, with camels carrying spices, a great quantity of gold, and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she talked with him about everything she had on her mind. Solomon answered all her questions; nothing was too hidden for the king to explain to her. When the queen of Sheba saw the full extent of Solomon’s wisdom, and the palace he had built, the food on his table, the seating of his officials, the service of his attendants and their robes, his cupbearers, and the burnt offerings he offered at the house of the LORD, she was left breathless. She said to the king, “It was true, the report that reached me in my own country about your words and your wisdom. But I did not believe what was said until I came and saw it with my own eyes. And indeed, I was not told even half. Your wisdom and prosperity go far beyond the report I heard. How happy your men must be! How happy are these officials of yours, who stand before you all the time and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loves Israel forever, he has made you king, to do justice and righteousness.” Then she gave the king about 9,000 pounds of gold, a very great quantity of spices, and precious stones. Never again did such an abundance of spices come in as the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Hiram’s fleet, which carried gold from Ophir, also brought from Ophir a great quantity of almug wood and precious stones. The king used the almug wood to make supports for the house of the LORD and the royal palace, as well as lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come in again or been seen to this day. King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she desired and asked for, on top of the gifts he had given her out of his royal bounty. Then she turned and went back to her own country, she and her servants.

Solomon’s wealth

The weight of the gold that came to Solomon in one year was about 50,000 pounds of gold, not counting what came from the traveling traders and the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold, with about 15 pounds of gold going into each shield. He also made 300 shields of beaten gold, with about 3 3/4 pounds of gold going into each shield. The king placed them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

Then the king made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, and the back of the throne had a rounded top. On either side of the seat were armrests, with two lions standing beside the armrests. Twelve lions stood there on the six steps, one at each end of each step. Nothing like it had ever been made for any kingdom. All King Solomon’s drinking cups were gold, and all the utensils in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. None were silver; in Solomon’s days silver was not thought of as anything. For the king had a fleet of Tarshish ships at sea along with Hiram’s fleet. Once every three years the Tarshish ships would come in, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes and peacocks. So King Solomon grew greater in riches and in wisdom than all the kings of the earth. The whole earth sought an audience with Solomon, to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart. Each of them brought a gift: articles of silver and gold, robes, weapons and spices, horses and mules, so much every year.

Solomon built up a force of chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, which he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah. Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s traders bought them from Kue at the going price. A chariot could be imported from Egypt for about 15 pounds of silver, and a horse for about 3 3/4 pounds. In the same way they exported them, through the king’s traders, to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.
