fields.summary: The queen of Sheba visits Solomon to test him with hard questions and praises his wisdom and God. Solomon’s wealth, gold and trade are described.

fields.title: 1 Kings 11
fields.body_html:
Solomon’s wives turn his heart

King Solomon loved many foreign women besides Pharaoh’s daughter: women of Moab, Ammon, Edom, Sidon, and the Hittites, from the nations the LORD had warned the Israelites about: “Do not intermarry with them, and do not let them intermarry with you, for they will surely turn your hearts to follow their gods.” Yet Solomon held fast to these women in love. He had 700 wives of royal birth and 300 concubines, and his wives turned his heart away. When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart to follow other gods, and his heart was not wholly devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of his father David had been. Solomon followed Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians and Milcom the detestable god of the Ammonites. So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not follow the LORD wholeheartedly, as his father David had done.

At that time Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the detestable god of Moab on the hill east of Jerusalem, and one for Molech the detestable god of the Ammonites. He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned offerings and sacrificed to their gods. The LORD became angry with Solomon, for his heart had turned from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had twice appeared to him and had commanded him about this very matter, that he must not follow other gods. But Solomon did not keep what the LORD had commanded.

Judgment on Solomon

So the LORD said to Solomon, “Since this is what you have done, and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I commanded you, I will certainly tear the kingdom from you and give it to your servant. Yet I will not do it in your lifetime, for the sake of your father David. I will tear it out of your son’s hand. But I will not tear away the whole kingdom. I will give your son one tribe because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, which I have chosen.” Then the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, who was of the royal family of Edom. Earlier, when David was at war with Edom, Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the dead and struck down every male in Edom; For Joab and all Israel stayed there six months, until he had destroyed every male in Edom. But Hadad escaped to Egypt with some Edomite officials who had served his father. Hadad was only a young boy at the time. They set out from Midian and came to Paran. Taking men with them from Paran, they came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt. Pharaoh provided Hadad with a house and food, and gave him land. Hadad won so much favor with Pharaoh that Pharaoh gave him his own wife’s sister in marriage, the sister of Queen Tahpenes. Tahpenes’ sister bore him a son, Genubath, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh’s palace. Genubath lived in Pharaoh’s household among Pharaoh’s own sons. While in Egypt, Hadad heard that David had rested with his ancestors and that Joab the commander of the army was dead. So Hadad said to Pharaoh, “Let me go, so that I may return to my own country.” Pharaoh said to him, “What do you lack here with me, that you now want to go back to your own country?” “Nothing,” Hadad answered, “but please let me go!” God also raised up another adversary against Solomon, Rezon son of Eliada, who had run away from his master, Hadadezer king of Zobah. He gathered men around him and became commander of a band of raiders after David slaughtered the forces of Zobah. They went to Damascus, settled there, and ruled in Damascus. Rezon was Israel’s adversary as long as Solomon lived, adding to the harm that Hadad did. He loathed Israel and reigned over Aram.

Ahijah’s word to Jeroboam

Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, was one of Solomon’s officials. His mother’s name was Zeruah, a widow. He rebelled against the king. This is how he came to rebel against the king. Solomon had built the Millo and closed up the gap in the wall of the City of David his father. Jeroboam was a strong and capable man. When Solomon saw how well the young man did his work, he put him in charge of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.

At that time, as Jeroboam was going out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road. Ahijah had on a new cloak, and the two were alone out in the country. Ahijah took hold of the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces. Then he said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces for yourself, for the LORD, the God of Israel, says this: ‘I am about to tear the kingdom out of Solomon’s hand and give you ten tribes, but one tribe will remain his because of my servant David and because of Jerusalem, the city I chose from among all the tribes of Israel, because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites. They have not followed my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rulings, as his father David did. Still, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand. I will keep him as leader all the days of his life, for the sake of my servant David, whom I chose and who kept my commandments and my statutes. But I will take the kingdom from his son’s hand and give you ten tribes of it. To his son I will give one tribe, so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city I have chosen for myself to put my name there. As for you, I will take you, and you will reign over all that you desire; you will be king over Israel. If you heed all that I command you, follow my ways, and do what is right in my sight by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as my servant David did, I will be with you. I will build you an enduring house, as I did for David, and I will make Israel yours. Because of this I will humble David’s descendants, but not forever.’”

Jeroboam flees, and Solomon dies

Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and stayed there until Solomon died. The rest of the acts of Solomon, all that he did and his wisdom, are written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon. Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years. Then Solomon rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David his father. And his son Rehoboam became king in his place.
fields.summary: Solomon loves many foreign wives, who turn his heart to other gods. God says the kingdom will be torn from his son, raises up adversaries, and the prophet Ahijah tells Jeroboam he will rule ten tribes; Solomon dies.

fields.title: 1 Kings 12
fields.body_html:
The northern tribes reject Rehoboam

Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had gathered at Shechem to make him king. When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about it, he was still in Egypt, where he had taken refuge from King Solomon, and he remained in Egypt. So they sent and summoned him, and Jeroboam and the whole assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam, “Your father made our yoke hard. Now ease the harsh labor your father demanded and the heavy yoke he laid on us, and we will serve you.” He said to them, “Go away for three days, then come back to me.” So the people left. King Rehoboam then consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was alive. “What answer do you advise me to give this people?” he asked. They answered him, “If today you will be a servant to this people and serve them, and answer them with kind words, they will always be your servants.” But he rejected the advice the elders had given him and consulted the young men who had grown up with him and now served him. He asked them, “What do you advise? How should we answer this people who have said to me, ‘Lighten the yoke your father put on us’?” The young men who had grown up with him answered, “This people said to you, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but you must make it lighter for us.’ Give them this answer: ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist. So then: my father laid a heavy yoke on you, but I will make your yoke heavier still. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.’” On the third day Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam, as the king had told them: “Return to me on the third day.” The king gave the people a harsh answer. He rejected the advice the elders had given him. He spoke to them as the young men had advised: “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will make your yoke heavier still. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.” So the king did not listen to the people, for this turn of events came from the LORD, to fulfill the word the LORD had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.
When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, the people answered the king:
“What part do we have in David?
We have no inheritance in Jesse’s son!
To your tents, Israel! Now look after your own house, David!”
So Israel went home.
But Rehoboam reigned over the Israelites who lived in the towns of Judah.

King Rehoboam then sent Adoram, the officer in charge of the forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam managed to get up into his chariot and escape to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.

Jeroboam becomes king of Israel

When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him, summoned him before the congregation, and made him king over all Israel. No one followed the house of David except the tribe of Judah alone. When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mustered the whole house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 picked warriors, to fight against the house of Israel and regain the kingdom for Rehoboam son of Solomon.

But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: “Speak to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to the whole house of Judah and Benjamin, and to everyone else among the people, and tell them, ‘The LORD says this: Do not go up to fight against your relatives, the Israelites. Go home, every one of you, for this thing has come from me.’” So they heeded the word of the LORD and went back home, as the LORD had said.

Jeroboam’s golden calves

Jeroboam fortified Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. From there he went out and fortified Penuel. Jeroboam thought to himself, “As things are, the kingdom will go back to the house of David. If these people go up to offer sacrifices at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to their lord, Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and go back to Rehoboam king of Judah.” So the king took counsel and made two golden calves. He said to the people, “You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Israel, here are your gods, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!” He set up one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan. This thing became a sin. The people went as far as Dan to worship before the one there. He also made shrines on the high places and appointed priests from all sorts of people, who were not Levites. Jeroboam instituted a festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the festival held in Judah, and he went up to the altar. He did this in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves he had made. And in Bethel he installed the priests of the high places he had made. He went up to the altar he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the month he had invented on his own. He instituted a festival for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense.
fields.summary: Rehoboam refuses to lighten the people’s burdens, and the ten northern tribes make Jeroboam king. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan so the people will not go to Jerusalem.

fields.title: 1 Kings 13
fields.body_html:
A man of God from Judah

Just then a man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the word of the LORD, while Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense. By the word of the LORD he cried out against the altar, “Altar, altar! The LORD says this: ‘A son will be born to the house of David, and his name will be Josiah. He will sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who burn their incense here, and human bones will be burned on you.’” That same day he gave a sign: “This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: The altar will be split apart, and the ashes on it will be poured out.” When King Jeroboam heard what the man of God had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!” But the hand he had stretched out against him withered, so that he could not pull it back. The altar was split apart, and the ashes poured out from the altar, in keeping with the sign that the man of God, by the word of the LORD, had given. Then the king said to the man of God, “Please plead with the LORD your God and pray for me, so that my hand may be restored to me.” So the man of God pleaded with the LORD, and the king’s hand was restored to him and became as it was before. Then the king said to the man of God, “Come to the palace with me and have something to eat, and I will give you a gift.” But the man of God answered the king, “Even if you gave me half your palace, I would not go in with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water in this place. For this is the command I was given by the word of the LORD: ‘Eat no bread and drink no water, and do not go back by the way you came.’” So he went another way and did not return by the road on which he had come to Bethel.

The old prophet of Bethel

Now an old prophet was living in Bethel. One of his sons came and told him everything the man of God had done in Bethel that day. His sons also told their father the words he had spoken to the king. Their father asked them, “Which way did he go?” His sons had seen which road the man of God from Judah had taken. “Saddle the donkey for me,” he told his sons. They saddled it for him, and he mounted and rode off. He followed the man of God and found him sitting under the terebinth. He asked him, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” “I am,” he replied. Then he said to him, “Come home with me and eat a meal.” He replied, “I cannot turn back with you or go home with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you here in this place. For a word came to me by the word of the LORD: ‘Eat no bread and drink no water there, and do not go back by the way you came.’” The old prophet said to him, “I am a prophet as well, just as you are, and by the word of the LORD an angel told me, ‘Bring him back with you to your house so that he can eat bread and drink water.’” But he was lying to him. So the man of God went back with him and ate bread and drank water in his house. As they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet, the very one who had brought him back. He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “The LORD says this: ‘You have defied the word of the LORD. Because you did not keep the command that the LORD your God gave you, and you came back and ate bread and drank water in the very place where he told you, “Do not eat bread or drink water,” your body will not be buried in the tomb of your ancestors.’” After the man of God had eaten bread and drunk, the old prophet saddled the donkey for him, the prophet he had brought back. He set off, and on the way a lion met him and killed him. His body lay thrown down on the road, with the donkey standing beside it, and the lion standing beside the body too. Some men passing by saw the body thrown down on the road and the lion standing beside the body. They went and told about it in the town where the old prophet lived. When the prophet who had brought him back from the road heard it, he said, “It is the man of God who defied the word of the LORD. The LORD has handed him over to the lion, and it has mauled him and killed him, in keeping with the word of the LORD that he spoke to him.” Then he said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me,” and they saddled it. He went and found the body thrown down on the road, and the donkey and the lion were standing beside it. The lion had neither eaten the body nor mauled the donkey. The prophet lifted the body of the man of God onto the donkey and brought it back. He came into the old prophet’s own town to mourn him and bury him. He laid the body in his own tomb, and they mourned over him, saying, “Oh, my brother!” After he had buried him, he said to his sons, “When I die, you are to bury me in the same tomb as the man of God. Put my bones beside his. What he cried out by the word of the LORD will certainly come true, both against the altar in Bethel and against every shrine on the high places in the towns of Samaria.”

Jeroboam’s sin continues

Even after this, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way. Instead he again appointed priests for the high places from all sorts of people. Anyone who wished, he ordained, and that man became one of the priests of the high places. This became the sin of the house of Jeroboam, and because of it the family was cut off and destroyed from the face of the earth.
fields.summary: A man of God from Judah denounces the altar at Bethel and the altar splits. Deceived by an old prophet, he disobeys God’s word and is killed by a lion.

fields.title: 1 Kings 14
fields.body_html:
Ahijah’s word against Jeroboam’s house

At that time Abijah son of Jeroboam fell ill. Jeroboam told his wife, “Please get up and change your appearance, so that no one will recognize you are Jeroboam’s wife, and go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet is there, the one who told me that I would be king over this people. Go to him with ten loaves of bread in your hand, some cakes and a jar of honey. He will tell you what is going to happen to the boy.” Jeroboam’s wife did so. She set out for Shiloh and arrived at the house of Ahijah. Ahijah was unable to see; his eyes had grown fixed with age.

But the LORD had said to Ahijah, “Jeroboam’s wife is coming to ask you for a word about her son, because he is sick. You are to tell her such and such. When she arrives, she will be pretending to be someone else.” As soon as Ahijah heard the sound of her footsteps at the doorway, he said, “Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why are you pretending to be someone else? I have been sent to you with hard news. Go and tell Jeroboam, ‘The LORD, the God of Israel, says this: I raised you up from among the people and made you ruler over my people Israel. I tore the kingdom out of the hands of David’s house and gave it to you. Yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments, who followed me wholeheartedly and did nothing but what was right in my sight. You have done more evil than all who were before you. You went and made yourself other gods, images of cast metal, to provoke me to anger, and you have thrown me behind your back.

Therefore I am about to bring disaster on Jeroboam’s house. From Jeroboam I will cut off every male in Israel, bond or free. I will burn away what remains of his house, the way someone burns up dung until none is left. Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city, the dogs will eat, and anyone who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat. For the LORD has spoken.’ As for you, get up and return to your house. The moment your feet enter the city, the child will die. All Israel will mourn for him and bury him. He is the only one belonging to Jeroboam who will be laid in a grave, because in him something good toward the LORD, the God of Israel, has been found in the house of Jeroboam. The LORD will raise up a king of his own over Israel, and that king will cut off Jeroboam’s house. This is the day; indeed, it has already begun. The LORD will strike Israel until it sways like a reed in the water. He will pull Israel up by the roots from this good land he gave their ancestors and scatter them beyond the Euphrates River, because they have made their Asherah poles and provoked the LORD to anger. He will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he committed and by which he led Israel to sin.” Then Jeroboam’s wife got up and left and came to Tirzah. As she was stepping over the threshold of the house, the boy died. They buried him, and all Israel mourned for him, just as the LORD had said through his servant Ahijah the prophet. The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he fought and how he reigned, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years. Then he rested with his ancestors, and his son Nadab became king in his place.

Rehoboam king of Judah

Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD had chosen from among all the tribes of Israel as the place for his name. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. By the sins they committed they stirred up his jealousy more than all their ancestors had done. They also built for themselves high places, standing stones and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every leafy tree. There were even male shrine prostitutes in the land. The people did all the detestable things of the nations that the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites.

Shishak attacks Jerusalem

In King Rehoboam’s fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He carried off the treasures of the house of the LORD and those of the king’s palace. He took everything, even all the gold shields Solomon had made. King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and entrusted them to the commanders of the guard who kept watch at the entrance of the king’s palace. Whenever the king went into the house of the LORD, the guards carried the shields, and afterward they brought them back to the guardroom. The rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days. Rehoboam rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite. His son Abijam became king in his place.
fields.summary: Ahijah tells Jeroboam’s wife that their son will die and Jeroboam’s house will be destroyed. In Judah Rehoboam’s people do evil, and Shishak of Egypt carries off the temple treasures.

fields.title: 1 Kings 15
fields.body_html:
Abijam king of Judah

In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king over Judah. He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. He walked in all the sins his father had committed before him, and his heart was not wholly given to the LORD his God, as the heart of his ancestor David had been. Yet for David’s sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son to rule after him and keeping Jerusalem secure, because David had done what was right in the sight of the LORD and had not turned aside from anything he commanded him as long as he lived, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life. The rest of the acts of Abijam, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. There was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. Then Abijam rested with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king in his place.

Asa king of Judah

In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa became king of Judah. He reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. Asa did what was right in the sight of the LORD, as his ancestor David had done. He drove the male shrine prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols his ancestors had made. He even deposed his mother Maacah as queen mother, because she had made a horrid image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it in the Kidron Valley. The high places, however, were not taken away. Even so, Asa’s heart was wholly given to the LORD all his life. He brought into the house of the LORD the gifts his father had dedicated and the gifts he himself had dedicated: silver, gold and utensils. There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel as long as they both lived. Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah, to keep anyone from going out or coming in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took all the silver and gold that was left in the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the treasuries of the king’s palace, and handed it over to his officials. King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion, the king of Aram, who ruled in Damascus, with this message: “Let there be a treaty between you and me, as there was between my father and your father. I am sending you a bribe of silver and gold. Go and break off your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, and he will withdraw from me.” Ben-hadad agreed with King Asa and sent the commanders of his forces out against the cities of Israel. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah and all Chinneroth, as well as all the land of Naphtali. When Baasha heard about it, he stopped building Ramah and stayed in Tirzah. Then King Asa called up all Judah, with no one exempt, and they carried away the stones and timber Baasha had used to build Ramah. With them King Asa fortified Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. The rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, all that he did and the cities he built, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. But in his old age he had a disease in his feet. Then Asa rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David his ancestor. His son Jehoshaphat became king in his place.

Nadab king of Israel

Nadab son of Jeroboam became king over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in his sin, by which he had led Israel to sin. Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, plotted against him and struck him down at Gibbethon, a town of the Philistines, while Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon. Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and became king in his place. As soon as he became king, he struck down the whole house of Jeroboam. He did not leave Jeroboam a single living soul, but destroyed them all, as the LORD had said through his servant Ahijah of Shiloh, because of Jeroboam’s sins, the sins he had committed and by which he had led Israel to sin, and by which he had provoked the LORD the God of Israel to anger. The rest of the acts of Nadab, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel as long as they both lived.

Baasha king of Israel

In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king over all Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin, by which he had led Israel to sin.
fields.summary: Abijam and Asa reign in Judah, and Asa removes idols. In Israel Nadab, Baasha and his house follow Jeroboam’s sins.

fields.title: 1 Kings 16
fields.body_html:
Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu son of Hanani, a word against Baasha: “I lifted you up from the dust and made you ruler over my people Israel. Yet you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and led my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins. So I am about to sweep away Baasha and his house after him, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat. Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city, the dogs will eat, and anyone of his who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat.” The rest of the acts of Baasha, what he did and his might, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Baasha rested with his ancestors and was buried in Tirzah, and his son Elah became king in his place. The word of the LORD had also come through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his house. It came because of all the evil Baasha did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger by the work of his hands, so that he became like the house of Jeroboam. It came also because he had struck that house down.

Elah and Zimri kings of Israel

In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years. His official Zimri, commander of half the chariots, plotted against him. Elah was in Tirzah at the time, getting drunk in the house of Arza, the steward of the palace in Tirzah. Zimri came in and struck him down, killing him in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and he became king in his place. As soon as he became king and sat on his throne, he struck down the whole house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male, neither his family redeemers nor his friends. So Zimri destroyed the whole house of Baasha, as the word of the LORD had said against Baasha through Jehu the prophet, because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of his son Elah, the sins they committed and by which they led Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols. The rest of the acts of Elah, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri became king in Tirzah, and he reigned seven days. The troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines. When the troops in the camp heard it said, “Zimri has plotted, and he has even struck down the king,” all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that very day in the camp. Then Omri and all Israel with him went up from Gibbethon and laid siege to Tirzah. When Zimri saw that the city had been taken, he went into the citadel of the royal palace and set the palace on fire over himself, and he died, because of the sins he had committed, doing what was evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam and in the sin he committed, by which he led Israel to sin. The rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy he carried out, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel.

Omri king of Israel

Then the people of Israel were split in two. Half the people followed Tibni son of Ginath, to make him king, and the other half followed Omri. But the people who followed Omri were stronger than the people who followed Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.

In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri became king over Israel, and he reigned twelve years, six of them in Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for about 150 pounds of silver. He built a city on the hill and named it Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill. Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He did more evil than all who were before him. He walked in all the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sin, by which he led Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols. The rest of the acts of Omri, what he did and the might he showed, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. Omri rested with his ancestors and was buried in Samaria, and his son Ahab became king in his place.

Ahab king of Israel

Ahab son of Omri became king over Israel in the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, and Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. Ahab son of Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him. As though walking in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat were a small thing for him, he married Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and he went and served Baal and bowed down to him. He set up an altar to Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria. Ahab also made the Asherah pole. He did more than all the kings of Israel before him to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger. In Ahab’s days Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho. At the price of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the price of Segub his youngest he set its gates in place, as the word of the LORD had said through Joshua son of Nun.
fields.summary: Israel’s kings Elah, Zimri, Omri and Ahab follow one another, each doing evil. Ahab marries Jezebel and serves Baal, and Jericho is rebuilt.

fields.title: 1 Kings 17
fields.body_html:
Elijah announces a drought

Elijah the Tishbite, one of the settlers in Gilead, said to Ahab, “As surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, whom I serve, there will be neither dew nor rain in the years ahead unless I give the word.”

Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah: “Leave this place and turn east. Hide by the Wadi Cherith, east of the Jordan. You will drink from the stream, and I have ordered the ravens to bring you food there.” So Elijah did as the LORD had told him. He went and stayed by the Wadi Cherith, east of the Jordan. The ravens brought him bread and meat every morning and every evening, and he drank from the stream. After a while the stream dried up, because there had been no rain in the land.

The widow of Zarephath

Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah: “Get up and go to Zarephath, a town of Sidon, and stay there. I have commanded a widow there to provide for you.” So he got up and went to Zarephath. When he came to the town gate, there was a widow gathering sticks. He called to her, “Please bring me a little water in a cup so I can drink.” As she was going to get it, he called after her, “Please bring a piece of bread with you too.” She said, “As surely as the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked, only a handful of flour in the jar and a little oil in the jug. I am gathering a couple of sticks so I can go home and prepare it for my son and me. We will eat it, and then we will die.” Elijah said to her, “Do not be afraid. Go and do what you said. But first bake me a small loaf from what you have and bring it out to me. After that, make something for yourself and your son.

For the LORD, the God of Israel, says this: ‘The jar of flour will not be emptied, and the jug of oil will not give out, until the day the LORD sends rain on the land.’” She went and did as Elijah had said, and she and he and her household had food to eat for many days. The jar of flour was not emptied, and the jug of oil did not give out, just as the LORD had said through Elijah.

Elijah raises the widow’s son

Some time after this, the son of the woman who owned the house fell ill. His illness grew so severe that at last there was no breath left in him. She said to Elijah, “What do you have against me, man of God? You came to me to bring my sin to light and to kill my son!” “Give me your son,” he said to her. He took the boy from her arms, carried him up to the upstairs room where he was staying, and put him down on his own bed. Then he cried out to the LORD, “The LORD my God, have you brought disaster even on this widow who has given me a place to stay, by causing her son to die?” Then he stretched himself out over the boy three times and cried out to the LORD, “The LORD my God, please let this boy’s life come back into him!” The LORD listened to Elijah’s cry, and the boy’s life came back into him, and he lived. Elijah took the boy, brought him down from the upstairs room into the house, and gave him to his mother. “Look,” Elijah said, “your son is alive!” Then the woman said to Elijah, “Now I know you are a man of God, and that what the LORD says through you is true.”
fields.summary: Elijah announces a drought and is fed by ravens at the Wadi Cherith. At Zarephath a widow’s flour and oil do not run out, and Elijah raises her son.

fields.title: 1 Kings 18
fields.body_html:
Elijah and Obadiah

After many days, in the third year, the LORD spoke to Elijah: “Go and appear before Ahab, and I will send rain on the land.” So Elijah went to present himself to Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria. Ahab summoned Obadiah, who was in charge of the palace. (Obadiah was a man who deeply revered the LORD. When Jezebel was killing off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah had taken a hundred of them and hidden them in caves, fifty in each, and had kept them supplied with food and water.) Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land to every spring and every stream bed. Perhaps we can find grass and keep the horses and mules alive, and not have to destroy any of our animals.” So they divided the land between them to cover it, Ahab going one way on his own and Obadiah another way on his own. As Obadiah was on his way, there was Elijah coming to meet him. Obadiah recognized him, bowed down with his face to the ground, and said, “Is it really you, my lord Elijah?” He answered him, “It is. Go and tell your master, ‘Elijah is here.’” Obadiah said, “What sin have I committed, that you are handing your servant over to Ahab to be put to death? As surely as the LORD your God lives, my master has sent people to look for you in every nation and kingdom. Whenever a nation said, ‘He is not here,’ he made its people swear that they could not find you. And now you are telling me, ‘Go and tell your master, “Elijah is here.”‘ As soon as I leave you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you off to some place I do not know. Then when I come and tell Ahab, and he cannot find you, he will kill me. Yet I, your servant, have revered the LORD since I was young. Has my lord not been told what I did when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the LORD? I hid a hundred of the LORD’s prophets, fifty in each of two caves, and kept them supplied with food and water. And now you are telling me, ‘Go and tell your master, “Elijah is here.”‘ He will kill me!”

Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel

Elijah said, “As surely as the LORD of Armies lives, whom I serve, I will present myself to Ahab today.” So Obadiah went off to meet Ahab and told him, and Ahab set out to meet Elijah. When Ahab saw Elijah, he said to him, “Is it you, you troubler of Israel?” Elijah answered, “I have not brought trouble on Israel. You have, you and your father’s house, because you have abandoned the LORD’s commandments and followed the Baals. Now send word and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, together with the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah who eat at Jezebel’s table.” So Ahab sent word to all the Israelites and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel. Elijah stepped up before all the people and said, “How long will you go on hobbling between two choices? If the LORD is God, follow him. If it is Baal, follow Baal.” But the people said nothing in reply. Then Elijah said to the people, “I am the only one left of the LORD’s prophets, but Baal has 450 prophets. Have two bulls brought to us. Let the prophets of Baal pick one of the bulls for themselves, cut it up, and set it on the wood, without lighting a fire. I will get the other bull ready and set it on the wood, and I too will light no fire. Then you call on your god by name, and I will call on the name of the LORD. Whichever god answers with fire, he is God.” All the people answered, “That is well said.” Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Choose one of the bulls for yourselves and prepare it first, since there are many of you. Call on your god by name, but light no fire.” So they took the bull that was given to them and prepared it. Then they called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, crying, “Baal, answer us!” But no sound came, and no one answered. And they kept hobbling in a dance around the altar they had made. At noon Elijah began to mock them. “Call out at the top of your voices!” he said. “He is a god, is he not? Maybe he is lost in thought, or he has stepped aside, or he has gone off on a trip. Or maybe he has fallen asleep, and must be woken up!” So they shouted louder and, as was their practice, slashed themselves with swords and spears until the blood flowed over them. Midday passed, and they went on raving in prophetic frenzy until the time for the evening offering. But there was no sound, no answer, no one taking notice. Then Elijah said to all the people, “Come here to me.” When they had all come near, he repaired the LORD’s altar, which had been torn down. Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe descended from the sons of Jacob, the man to whom the word of the LORD had come: “Your name will be Israel.” He used the stones to build an altar in the name of the LORD, and around the altar he dug a trench large enough to hold about 13 quarts of seed. He arranged the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and laid it on the wood. Then he said, “Fill four jars with water and pour it over the burnt offering and the wood.” “Again,” he said, and they did it again. “Once more,” he said, and they did it a third time. The water ran down all around the altar, and he also filled the trench with water. At the time of the evening offering, Elijah the prophet stepped forward and said, “The LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, today make it known that you are God in Israel, that I am your servant, and that it is at your word that I have done all this. Answer me, the LORD, answer me, so that these people may know that you, the LORD, are God and are turning their hearts back again.” Then fire from the LORD fell. It burned up the burnt offering, the wood, the stones and the soil, and licked up the water in the trench. When all the people saw it, they fell face down and said, “The LORD, he is God! The LORD, he is God!” Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal. Do not let one of them get away!” They seized them, and Elijah took them down to the Kishon River and put them to death there. Then Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink. There is the sound of a roaring downpour.” So Ahab went up to eat and drink, while Elijah climbed to the top of Carmel. He bowed down to the ground and put his face between his knees. He said to his servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” The servant went up and looked, and said, “There is nothing there.” Seven times Elijah told him, “Go back.” The seventh time the servant said, “Look, a cloud as small as a man’s hand is rising out of the sea.” Elijah said, “Go up and tell Ahab, ‘Hitch up your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’” Meanwhile, in a very short time, the sky grew black with clouds and wind, and a heavy rain came. Ahab rode off and went to Jezreel. The hand of the LORD came on Elijah. He tucked his robe into his belt and ran in front of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.
fields.summary: Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, and fire falls from God to consume his sacrifice. The prophets of Baal are killed, and the rain returns.

fields.title: 1 Kings 19
fields.body_html:
Elijah flees to Horeb

Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, including how he had put all the prophets to the sword. So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah to say, “May the gods deal with me ever so severely if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them.” When Elijah saw how things stood, he got up and fled for his life. He reached Beersheba, in Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went on a day’s journey into the wilderness. He came to a broom tree and sat down under it, and he prayed that he might die. “It is enough,” he said. “Now, LORD, take my life, for I am no better than my ancestors.” Then he lay down and slept under the broom tree. And all at once an angel touched him and said to him, “Get up and eat.” He looked, and there by his head was a loaf baked on hot stones and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and then lay down again. The angel of the LORD came back a second time, touched him and said, “Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you.” So he got up, ate and drank, and in the strength of that food he walked forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God. There he came to the cave and spent the night in it. Then the word of the LORD came to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He answered, “I have been very zealous for the LORD God of Armies, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant. They have torn down your altars and put your prophets to the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.” The LORD said, “Go out and stand on the mountain in the presence of the LORD.” And there, the LORD was passing by. A mighty, fierce wind was splitting the mountains and smashing the rocks to pieces ahead of the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind came an earthquake; the LORD was not in the earthquake. Then came fire after the earthquake, but the LORD was not in the fire. And when the fire had passed, a faint sound, thin as silence. When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his cloak around his face, went out, and stood at the cave’s mouth. Then a voice came to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” He answered, “I have been very zealous for the LORD God of Armies, because the Israelites have abandoned your covenant. They have torn down your altars and put your prophets to the sword. I alone am left, and now they are seeking to take my life.”

The call of Elisha

The LORD said to him, “Go back the way you came, and go to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael as king over Aram. Anoint Jehu son of Nimshi as king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to be prophet in your place. Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu will put to death, and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha will put to death. Yet I will leave 7,000 in Israel, everyone whose knees have not bent to Baal and whose lips have not kissed him.” So Elijah went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat plowing. There were twelve pairs of oxen ahead of him, and he was with the twelfth pair. Elijah went over to him and threw his cloak over him. Then Elisha left the oxen, ran after Elijah and said, “Let me kiss my father and my mother goodbye, please, and then I will follow you.” Elijah said to him, “Go back. What have I done to you?” Elisha turned back from following him. He took the pair of oxen and slaughtered them, boiled their meat using the oxen’s gear for fuel, and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he got up, followed Elijah and became his attendant.
fields.summary: Fleeing Jezebel, Elijah asks to die in the wilderness and is fed by an angel. At Horeb God speaks to him in a quiet voice and sends him to anoint new kings and Elisha, who leaves his oxen to follow him.

fields.title: 1 Kings 20
fields.body_html:
Ben-hadad besieges Samaria

Ben-hadad king of Aram gathered his whole army. Thirty-two kings were with him, along with horses and chariots. He marched up, laid siege to Samaria, and attacked it. He sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel, and said to him, “Ben-hadad says this: ‘Your silver and your gold are mine, and the best of your wives and children are mine as well.’” The king of Israel answered, “It is as you say, my lord the king. I am yours, with all that I have.” The messengers came back and said, “Ben-hadad says this: ‘I sent you word that you must hand over to me your silver and gold, your wives and your children, but about this time tomorrow I will send my officials to you, and they will search your palace and the houses of your officials. They will lay their hands on everything you value and carry it off.’” Then the king of Israel called in all the elders of the land and told them, “Look and see how this man is out to do us harm! He sent to me for my wives and my children, my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him.” All the elders and all the people told him, “Do not listen to him, and do not give in.” So he told Ben-hadad’s messengers, “Tell my lord the king, ‘I will do everything you demanded of your servant the first time, but this I cannot do.’” The messengers left and took the answer back to Ben-hadad. Then Ben-hadad sent him this message: “May the gods deal with me ever so severely if Samaria’s dust is enough to give a handful to each of the troops who follow me!” The king of Israel answered, “Tell him: ‘The man buckling his armor on should not brag like the man unbuckling it.’” Ben-hadad heard this reply while he and the kings were drinking in their shelters. He said to his officials, “Take your positions!” So they took up positions against the city. Just then a prophet came up to Ahab king of Israel and said, “The LORD says this: ‘Do you see this whole huge army? I am handing it over to you today, and then you will know that I am the LORD.’” Ahab asked, “By whom?” He answered, “The LORD says this: ‘By the young men of the provincial officials.’” Ahab asked, “Who will start the battle?” He answered, “You will.” So Ahab mustered the young men of the provincial officials, 232 of them. After them he mustered all the troops, all the Israelites, 7,000 in all. They marched out at noon, while Ben-hadad was getting drunk in the shelters with the thirty-two kings who were his allies. The young men of the provincial officials went out first. Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, “Men are coming out of Samaria.” He said, “If they have come out to make peace, take them alive. If they have come out to fight, take them alive.” So these went out from the city: the young men of the provincial officials, and the army behind them. Each of them struck down his man. The Arameans fled, and Israel chased them, but Ben-hadad king of Aram escaped on horseback with some horsemen. The king of Israel went out and attacked the horses and chariots, and inflicted a heavy defeat on the Arameans. Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said to him, “Go and build up your strength. Think carefully about what you must do, because in the spring the king of Aram will march against you.”

Israel defeats Aram at Aphek

Meanwhile the officials of the king of Aram advised him, “Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were too strong for us. But let us fight them on the plain, and we will certainly be stronger than they are. And do this: remove each of the kings from his post, and put governors in their place. Then raise an army for yourself like the army you lost, horse for horse and chariot for chariot, and let us fight them on the plain. We will certainly be stronger than they are.” He took their advice and did so.

In the spring Ben-hadad mustered the Arameans and marched up to Aphek to fight against Israel. The Israelites were mustered and given supplies, and they went out to meet them. The Israelites camped facing them like two little flocks of goats, while the Arameans filled the whole land. Then the man of God came to the king of Israel and said, “The LORD says this: ‘Because the Arameans have said that the LORD is a god of the hills and not a god of the valleys, I will hand this whole huge army over to you, and you will know that I am the LORD.’” For seven days the two armies camped opposite each other. On the seventh day the battle was joined, and the Israelites struck down 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in a single day. The rest fled into the town of Aphek, and the wall fell on 27,000 of the men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled into the town and hid in an inner room.

His officials said to him, “Listen, we have heard that the kings of Israel’s royal house are kings who show faithful love. Let us tie sackcloth around our waists and put ropes on our heads, and go out to Israel’s king. Perhaps he will spare your life.” So they tied sackcloth around their waists and ropes on their heads, came before the king of Israel, and told him, “Your servant Ben-hadad pleads, ‘Please spare my life.’” Ahab replied, “Is he still alive? He is my brother.” The men took this as a good sign and quickly seized on his word, saying, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad!” He said, “Go and bring him.” When Ben-hadad came out to him, Ahab had him come up into his chariot. Ben-hadad said to him, “I will give back the cities my father took from your father, and you may set up your own market streets in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria.” Ahab said, “On the terms of a treaty I will set you free.” So he made a treaty with him and let him go.

A prophet condemns Ahab

By the word of the LORD one of the company of prophets said to his companion, “Please strike me.” But the man would not strike him. So he said to him, “Because you have not obeyed the LORD, as soon as you leave me a lion will kill you.” And when he had left him, a lion found him and killed him. He found another man and said to him, “Please strike me.” This man struck him and left him wounded. Then the prophet went and waited for the king by the road. He disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes. As the king passed by, the prophet called out to him, “Your servant went out into the thick of the battle, and suddenly a man turned aside and brought me a prisoner. He said, ‘Guard this man. If he is ever missing, it will be your life for his life, or else you must pay about 75 pounds of silver.’ But while your servant was busy with this and that, the man was gone.” The king of Israel said to him, “That is your sentence. You have pronounced it yourself.” Then the man quickly took the bandage off his eyes, and the king of Israel knew him for one of the prophets. The prophet said to him, “The LORD says this: ‘Because you have let go the man I had devoted to destruction, your life will go for his life, and your people for his people.’” The king of Israel set off for his palace, sullen and angry, and came to Samaria.
fields.summary: Ben-hadad of Aram besieges Samaria, and a prophet promises Ahab victory twice over. Ahab spares Ben-hadad and is told that his life will be forfeit.

fields.title: 1 Kings 21
fields.body_html:
Naboth’s vineyard

Some time after these events, Naboth the Jezreelite owned a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab, the king of Samaria. Ahab said to Naboth, “Let me have your vineyard to use as a vegetable garden, since it is close to my palace. In its place I will give you a better vineyard, or, if you prefer, I will pay you its value in silver.” But Naboth said to Ahab, “The LORD forbid that I hand over to you the inheritance of my ancestors!” So Ahab went home sullen and angry because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him: “I will not give you the inheritance of my ancestors.” He lay down on his bed, turned his face away, and would not eat. His wife Jezebel came in and asked him, “Why are you so downcast that you will not eat?” He told her, “I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, ‘Sell me your vineyard, or if you prefer, I will give you another vineyard in its place.’ But he said, ‘I will not give you my vineyard.’” His wife Jezebel said to him, “Are you not the one who rules as king over Israel now? Get up and eat something, and cheer up. I myself will get you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite.” So she wrote letters in Ahab’s name and put his seal on them, and she sent them to the leading men and elders of Naboth’s city, who lived there with him. In the letters she wrote: “Proclaim a fast, and seat Naboth at the front of the people. Seat two worthless men opposite him, and have them bring this charge against him: ‘You have cursed God and the king.’ Then take him outside and stone him until he dies.” The men of Naboth’s city, the elders and leading men who lived there, did as Jezebel had instructed them, exactly as it was written in the letters she had sent them. They proclaimed a fast and seated Naboth at the front of the people. Then the two worthless men came in and sat opposite him, and the worthless men brought their charge against Naboth in front of the people: “Naboth has cursed God and the king.” So they led him out of the city and stoned him until he died. Then they sent a message to Jezebel: “Naboth has been stoned, and he is dead.” As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, she told Ahab, “Get up and take possession of the vineyard that Naboth the Jezreelite refused to sell you. Naboth is no longer alive. He is dead.” Once Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he rose and went down to Naboth the Jezreelite’s vineyard to take possession of it.

Elijah confronts Ahab

Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite: “Rise and go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who reigns in Samaria. He is in Naboth’s vineyard right now; he has gone down there to take possession of it. Say to him, ‘The LORD says this: Have you committed murder and also taken possession?’ Then say to him, ‘The LORD says this: In the place where the dogs licked up Naboth’s blood, the dogs will lick up your blood too, yes, yours.’” Ahab said to Elijah, “Have you found me, my enemy?” “I have found you,” Elijah answered, “because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the LORD. I am about to bring disaster on you. I will sweep away those who come after you, and I will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, bond or free. I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have provoked me to anger and have led Israel to sin. And concerning Jezebel the LORD has also spoken: ‘The dogs will eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.’ Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city, the dogs will eat, and anyone who dies in the open country, the birds of the sky will eat.” There was truly no one like Ahab, who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD, urged on by his wife Jezebel. He acted in the most detestable way by going after idols, just as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD drove out before the Israelites.

Ahab humbles himself

When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put sackcloth on his body, and fasted. He lay down in sackcloth and went about quietly.

Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite: “Have you noticed how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Since he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster during his lifetime. I will bring the disaster on his house in his son’s days.”
fields.summary: Ahab wants Naboth’s vineyard, and Jezebel has Naboth falsely accused and stoned. Elijah announces judgment on Ahab and Jezebel, and Ahab humbles himself.

fields.title: 1 Kings 22
fields.body_html:
Micaiah warns Ahab

For three years there was no war between Aram and Israel.

Then in the third year Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to visit Israel’s king. The king of Israel said to his officials, “You know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, yet we are doing nothing to take it back from the king of Aram.” He asked Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth-gilead?” Jehoshaphat answered the king of Israel, “I am as you are, my troops are as your troops, my horses as your horses.” But Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “First, please seek the word of the LORD.” So the king of Israel gathered the prophets, about four hundred men, and asked them, “Shall I go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I hold back?” “Go up,” they said, “for the Lord will give it into the king’s hand.” But Jehoshaphat said, “Is there no other prophet of the LORD here whom we can ask?” The king of Israel answered Jehoshaphat, “There is still one man through whom we could inquire of the LORD: Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, for his prophecies about me are never good, only bad.” Jehoshaphat said, “Let the king not speak like that.” So the king of Israel called one of his court officials and said, “Bring Micaiah son of Imlah at once.” Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, dressed in their royal robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance to the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying in front of them. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah had made himself iron horns, and he said, “The LORD says this: ‘With these you will gore the Arameans until they are destroyed.’” All the prophets were prophesying the same thing: “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and be victorious. The LORD will give it into the king’s hand.” The messenger who had gone to call Micaiah said to him, “Listen, the prophets are all speaking with one voice, and what they say is good for the king. Please let your word be like one of theirs, and speak favorably.” But Micaiah said, “As surely as the LORD lives, whatever the LORD says to me is what I will speak.” When he came to the king, the king asked him, “Micaiah, shall we go to war against Ramoth-gilead, or shall we hold back?” He answered, “Go up and be victorious. The LORD will give it into the king’s hand.” But the king said to him, “How often must I put you under oath to tell me only the truth in the name of the LORD?”
Then Micaiah said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills,
like sheep that have no shepherd.
And the LORD said, ‘These have no master;
let each of them go home in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not say to you that he prophesies nothing good about me, only bad?” Micaiah went on, “Then hear the word of the LORD. I saw the LORD seated on his throne, with all the host of heaven standing around him, on his right and on his left. The LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab to go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ Some suggested one thing and some another. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD and said, ‘I will entice him.’ The LORD asked him, ‘How?’ He said, ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ The LORD said, ‘You will entice him, and you will succeed. Go and do it.’ So now, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these prophets of yours. The LORD has decreed disaster for you.” Then Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came up and slapped Micaiah on the cheek. “Which way did the Spirit of the LORD take from me to speak to you?” he asked. Micaiah replied, “You will find out on the day you go into an inner room to hide.” Then the king of Israel ordered, “Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the city governor, and to Joash, the king’s son, and tell them, ‘The king says this: “Put this man in prison and feed him with scant bread and scant water until I come back safely.”‘” Micaiah said, “If you ever come back safely, the LORD has not spoken through me.” And he added, “Listen, all you peoples!” So the king of Israel went up to Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat king of Judah with him. The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will go into the battle in disguise, but you should put on your royal robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into the fight. Now the king of Aram had given an order to his thirty-two chariot commanders: “Fight with no one, small or great, but the king of Israel alone.” When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “Surely that is the king of Israel!” So they turned to attack him, and Jehoshaphat cried out. Once the chariot commanders saw he was not Israel’s king, they broke off the chase. But a man drew his bow at random and hit the king of Israel between the joints of his scale armor and the breastplate. The king said to his chariot driver, “Turn around and get me out of the battle, because I am wounded.” All that day the battle grew fiercer, and the king was held upright in his chariot facing the Arameans. He died at evening, and blood from the wound flowed down into the floor of the chariot. As the sun was setting, a shout went through the army: “Every man to his town! Every man to his own land!” So the king died. He was brought to Samaria, and they buried him there. When they washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes bathed there, just as the LORD had said. The rest of the acts of Ahab, all that he did, the ivory palace he built and all the cities he built, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Israel. So Ahab rested with his ancestors, and his son Ahaziah became king in his place.

Jehoshaphat king of Judah

In the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel, Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king over Judah. Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king. He reigned in Jerusalem twenty-five years, and his mother’s name was Azubah daughter of Shilhi. He followed all the ways of his father Asa and did not turn aside from them, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. However, the high places were not removed; the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places. Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel. The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, the might he showed and how he waged war, are written in the Book of the History of the Kings of Judah. He also drove out of the land the rest of the male shrine prostitutes who were left from the days of his father Asa. There was then no king in Edom; a deputy ruled as king. Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to sail to Ophir for gold, but they never sailed, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber. Then Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, “Let my men sail with your men in the ships.” But Jehoshaphat refused. Then Jehoshaphat rested with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David his ancestor. His son Jehoram became king in his place.

Ahaziah king of Israel

In the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Ahaziah son of Ahab became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned over Israel two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He followed the ways of his father and his mother, and the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. He served Baal and worshiped him, and he provoked the LORD the God of Israel to anger, as his father had.
fields.summary: Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah plan war against Aram. The prophet Micaiah foretells disaster, Ahab is killed in battle, and Jehoshaphat and Ahaziah reign.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
He served Baal and worshiped him, and he provoked the LORD the God of Israel to anger, as his father had.

— 1 Kings 22:53

1 Kings does not end; it breaks off. Its last sentence describes a new king doing exactly what his father did, and the story runs straight on into 2 Kings. The book that opened with the glory of Solomon closes with the son of Ahab bowing to Baal. Somewhere between the two, the golden age slipped away.

The question the book leaves with you

Almost every king in 1 Kings fails. Solomon, the wisest of them, ends with a divided heart. Jeroboam, given ten tribes by a prophet’s word, makes golden calves to keep them. Ahab, warned by drought and fire and a voice at his own vineyard, goes into battle in disguise rather than listen. The best of Judah’s kings, Asa and Jehoshaphat, do what is right, yet leave the high places standing. The book’s verdict on the monarchy is not that it lacked power, but that it lacked a whole heart.

And so it leaves a question that is older than the monarchy: whom will you follow? Elijah put it to a crowd on Carmel, “How long will you go on hobbling between two choices?”, and the people said nothing. The book will not let its readers stay silent. Every reign ends with a verdict, and readers are meant to ask what the verdict on their own lives would be.

Yet the book also leaves two small lights burning. One is the lamp God promised to keep for David in Jerusalem, “so that my servant David may always have a lamp before me”, a promise that outlasts every bad king of Judah. The other is the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal, unknown even to Elijah. God’s purposes did not depend on the kings. They never had.

Where the story goes next

2 Kings carries the story on: Elijah taken up in a whirlwind, his cloak falling to Elisha, the end of Ahab’s house, the fall of Samaria and at last of Jerusalem itself. The man of God’s word against Jeroboam’s altar comes true when Josiah burns bones on it, three centuries after it was spoken.

But the New Testament reaches back into 1 Kings again and again. Jesus pointed to the queen of Sheba, who travelled so far to hear Solomon, and said:

The queen from the south will stand up on judgment day alongside this generation and condemn it. She traveled from the far edges of the earth to listen to Solomon’s wisdom. Yet here is something greater than Solomon.

— Matthew 12:42

Solomon prayed that God would hear those who prayed toward the house he had built; Jesus, standing in the temple, spoke of a temple that would be torn down and raised in three days, “But the temple he meant was his own body.” Stephen, before the council, remembered that “it was Solomon who built a house for him”, and added, as Solomon himself had, that the Most High does not live in houses made by hands (Acts 7:47–48).

Elijah too steps out of this book into the Gospels. John the Baptist came “in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers back to their children” (Luke 1:17). On the mountain of the transfiguration Elijah and Moses appeared with Jesus and spoke of “the exodus he was about to complete in Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). The prophet who fled to Horeb, sure he alone was left, stood at last beside the one he had been waiting for.

Where to go from here

The preachers of the church have loved these chapters, Elijah’s above all. A few places to begin:

  • On Solomon and his kingdom (1 Kings 1–11). Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “1 Kings and 2 Chronicles: The Kingdom of Peace” reads Solomon’s reign of peace as a picture of the rest Christ gives; Hudson Taylor’s sermon Coming to the King (1 Kings 10:13), on the queen of Sheba’s journey as a pattern for coming to Christ; and Book XVII of Augustine’s The City of God, which argues that the promises made to David’s son are not fulfilled in Solomon but in Christ.
  • On Elijah and the drought (1 Kings 17–18). E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, with its chapter “Elijah, the Praying Prophet”; and “Fire from Heaven, Rain on the Earth”, a chapter of The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original, on Elijah’s prayers on Carmel.
  • On Elijah at Horeb (1 Kings 19). Alexander Maclaren’s sermon Elijah’s Weakness, and Its Cure (1 Kings 19:1–18), on God’s gentle care of a burnt-out servant; A. B. Simpson’s sermon The Power of Stillness (1 Kings 19:12); and the chapter “The Still, Small Voice” in Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High.
  • For younger readers. Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets, an Ochorus Original, which retells Solomon’s request for wisdom, Elijah and the ravens, the fire on the mountain and the still, small voice.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 Kings in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read on into 2 Kings, remembering the words Solomon spoke on the day the temple was dedicated, words the rest of the story would test to the limit and never disprove:

“Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to his people Israel, just as he promised. Of all the good promises he made through his servant Moses, not one word has failed.

— 1 Kings 8:56
